Burning barricades and clashes with riot police erupted in Barcelona after a peaceful march against soaring housing costs. Police used projectiles to disperse masked protesters as violence spread through the city centre.

Shortly after 7.30 pm, on Wednesday 11 November, groups of masked protesters began throwing stones, bottles and fireworks at police near Passeig de Gràcia and Plaça de Catalunya. Rubbish bins and street furniture were set alight, creating burning barricades in the city centre, while shop windows were smashed and stores reportedly looted.

Footage shows flames engulfing barricades and protesters confronting riot police, who responded with crowd-control projectiles and baton charges. Catalonia's Mossos d'Esquadra police moved to disperse the groups as the disturbances spread towards Las Ramblas.

Violent clashes broke out after an otherwise peaceful mass demonstration, when small groups of masked youths broke away from the main crowd. Municipal police estimated that more than 55,000 people had taken part, while organisers put the figure closer to 400,000. As night fell, rioters smashed shopfronts, set rubbish bins alight and threw objects at officers from the Mossos d'Esquadra, Catalonia's regional police force. Eighteen people were arrested during the unrest, bringing the day's total to 20. Catalan President Salvador Illa condemned the violence, stressing that it did not reflect the spirit of the peaceful protest.

The unrest unfolded during Spain’s first 24-hour general strike since 2012, a nationwide stoppage trade unions claim mobilised around four million workers. The protest mirrors a broader wave of social discontent over housing affordability, stagnant wages, and inflation that has swept through Portugal, Belgium, France, Italy, and Germany in recent months. Coming less than three weeks before the 29 November snap election, the unrest places immense political pressure on the government.

Marking the 108th anniversary of the 1918 armistice, Emmanuel Macron led the ceremony at the Arc de Triomphe, while Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon chose symbolic venues to deliver their messages months before the presidential election.

France commemorated this Wednesday the end of the fighting of the First World War. As every year, the 11 November ceremonies brought together elected officials, members of the armed forces, veterans and citizens around war memorials across the country. But this year's events inevitably had a political dimension, with several contenders in the presidential election taking part, each choosing their own location and message.

In Paris, Emmanuel Macron presided over the national ceremony under the Arc de Triomphe. It was his last 11 November as head of state. The president first paid tribute to Georges Clemenceau, laying a wreath in front of his statue on the Champs-Élysées, before heading to Place de l'Étoile. After reviewing the troops, he rekindled the flame of the Unknown Soldier and observed a minute's silence.

The names of five service members who have died for France since the start of the year were then read out. Among them were adjudant-chef Thibaud Breteau, who died in the Levant, major Arnaud Frion, killed in Iraq, as well as three soldiers who died in Lebanon: adjudant Florian Montorio, sergent Anicet Girardin and caporal-chef Florian Gillet.

La Marseillaise was then sung by the army choir.

The head of state did not speak during the ceremony. However, he posted on X, stating that "Le Bleuet de France is the memory of those who have died for France. It expresses our solidarity with those who still bear the scars of History," and adding that "behind every uniform, there is courage. Behind every sacrifice, a family. Behind every hero, France that remembers."

In Hénin-Beaumont, Marine Le Pen calls for national unity

It was in her stronghold of Pas-de-Calais that Marine Le Pen chose to commemorate 11 November. The RN presidential candidate paid tribute to soldiers killed in action, but also to the women who remained on the home front during the conflict.

In her speech, she stressed the need to preserve collective memory and keep alive the sense of national belonging. "Honouring their memory, we commit ourselves to preserving the values for which they fought: sovereignty, freedom and love for our homeland."

Evoking the spirit of resistance and sense of duty of the Poilus, the name given to French soldiers during WW1, Marine Le Pen called for collective action in the face of hardship: "Faced with the misfortunes of the country, we cannot remain spectators or commentators," insisting that national cohesion cannot be built on a loss of bearings or on amnesia.

In Creuse, Jean-Luc Mélenchon chooses a pacifist monument

For his part, Jean-Luc Mélenchon opted for a less conventional trip. The La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) leader travelled to Gentioux-Pigerolles, in the Creuse department, centre of France, to take part in the ceremony in front of the village war memorial. This is a highly symbolic site, known for its inscription "Cursed be war". The monument depicts an orphan raising his fist towards the names of soldiers killed in combat, as shown in a photo in this post on the presidential candidate's X account.

A tribute marked by pacifism and anti-militarism, which makes Gentioux-Pigerolles a rallying point for activists committed to these ideas.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon's choice is therefore no accident. The France Unbowed candidate, who had already visited the site in the past, framed his speech around remembrance and a rejection of war.

"I come here because, like many others, I believe that whoever does not know their history and has not reflected on it is exposed to seeing it repeat itself, without being able to recognise its features when it comes. It is our mission, we Unbowed, to carry History," he said.

He also hammered home his opposition to any preparation for conflict: "Down with war! We will not wage it, we will not organise it, we will not prepare it!", a pacifist message that echoes his recent statements on Ukraine.

At a rally last Saturday in Le Bourget, Jean-Luc Mélenchon defended the idea of "consulting" the inhabitants of Donbas, largely occupied by the Russian army, about their future, as part of a settlement of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

This proposal earned him a firm response from Ukrainian diplomacy, which recalled that Ukrainians, including the inhabitants of Donbas, had already chosen their borders at the 1991 independence referendum.

This Wednesday in Gentioux-Pigerolles, the France Unbowed leader also called for national unity, which he considers inseparable from that of the French people, while denouncing racism and hatred of others.

Citizens face burdens and service cuts, while the federal government spends millions on furniture, lamps and decor, claims the Taxpayers' Association.

Since the start of the current legislative term in May 2025, the federal government has spent around 5.8 million euros on new furniture, furnishings and decorations. This emerges from a government response to a parliamentary question from the AfD group in the Bundestag.

The figures have now triggered sharp criticism from the German Taxpayers' Association.

Its president, Reiner Holznagel, is particularly critical of what he sees as a contradiction between calls for savings directed at the public and the spending within the machinery of government.

"There is supposedly no room to relieve the burden on citizens, but when it comes to their own government apparatus, the belt is pretty loose - for decor and the like!", Holznagel told the German newspaper Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung.

Foreign Office, Defence and Finance most spending

Spending by the 16 federal ministries has totalled about 5.8 million euros since May 2025. The figures cover not only classic items of furniture but also lamps, carpets, curtains, paintings, sculptures and ornamental plants.

The Foreign Office was particularly free with its money. There, spending on furniture, lamps, carpets and decoration has added up to €840,062 since the start of the legislative term. In 2026 alone, around €256,000 went on lamps, carpets and curtains.

In second place comes the Defence Ministry with around €813,000. The Federal Finance Ministry has also recorded substantial expenditure. Since May 2025, the department led by Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) has invested more than half a million euros in furniture, equipment and decoration.

Finance Ministry tops the league

Particularly striking is a look at decoration costs alone. Here, the Finance Ministry heads the list. Since May 2025, it has spent a total of €45,077 on decorations. That means more than a quarter of the federal government's total decoration spending is accounted for by this ministry.

The Finance Ministry has also incurred substantial costs for office furnishings at the senior management level. In 2026 alone, 47,737 euros have so far been spent on refitting the relevant offices.

Taxpayers' association calls for more responsible spending policy

For the German Taxpayers' Association, the figures are a reason to question the federal government's spending policy in principle. Holznagel argues that anyone demanding thrift from citizens must apply the same standards within their own authorities and ministries.

He sees the Bundestag's budget committee as having a particular responsibility. It can now demonstrate how seriously politicians take the savings measures they have announced.

The debate is likely to raise the broader question of how responsibly the federal government handles taxpayers' money. Especially at a time of strained public finances, the public is likely to watch closely how politicians spend their money.

Few places in Ukraine suffer more from Russia's invasion. Zaporizhzhia mayor Regina Kharchenko tells Euronews about winter, attacks on civilians and the Russian-held nuclear plant.

For the residents of Zaporizhzhia, Russian attacks have become a sad part of everyday life. The city lies only 20 kilometres from the front line. At the beginning of the month, several glide bombs hit an underground school in the village of Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region. Civilians had gathered there for the distribution of humanitarian aid. At least 50 people were killed.

Time and again, Russian units attack civilian targets here. In October, a Russian drone hit a minibus at a stop in the city centre. Three people were injured, according to the independent Ukrainian outlet Ukrainska Pravda. Four people were wounded in another drone strike on a bus.

But the greatest danger lies just outside the city: the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant. It has been in the hands of Russian forces since March 2022. So far this year, the external power supply has already failed 16 times. The most recent incident was only a few days ago. Once again, the plant had to be cooled using emergency generators.

Regina Kharchenko has been acting mayor of the city since April 2024. She was born in Crimea, which has been annexed by Russia since 2014. As a child, the lawyer moved to Zaporizhzhia. In Berlin, she represents her city at the 21st Kyiv Dialogue, a cross-party German-Ukrainian dialogue platform that brings together politics, the media and civil society.

In an interview with Euronews, the politician talks about the coming winter, Russian attacks on critical infrastructure and European aid to Ukraine.

Euronews: Almost every day, Zaporizhzhia is attacked by Russia. How does it feel for you to be so far away in Berlin right now, and what are you hoping to achieve with your visit?

Kharchenko: First of all, I consider it a great honour to be able to represent Zaporizhzhia. I can talk about real life in wartime and explain to people that this is a very difficult life experience that many Ukrainians would gladly do without. But even here, even while I am speaking on the panel, I am involved in all ongoing operations.

Just today, a residential building in our city was badly damaged; its structure is at risk of collapse, and unfortunately, one person was injured. But all municipal services and everyone tasked with helping people are already on site. Wherever I am, I coordinate what is happening in Zaporizhzhia and am of course reachable. I expect, first, that this panel will allow German and Polish municipalities to take away important information for themselves. And second, we have already received concrete offers of humanitarian aid so that people can get through this winter.

Euronews: You spoke at the Kyiv Dialogue on a forum about resilience within civil society. How have the residents of Zaporizhzhia become so resilient?

Kharchenko: Above all, society is resilient because every municipality has to prepare its area for winter. The city has to guarantee heating and water supplies and try to get the problems with the power supply under control. That is extremely important for us. In addition, socially vulnerable groups and internally displaced people need more support.

In Zaporizhzhia alone, more than 200,000 internally displaced people are living, and that, too, is a challenge for us. Resilience, therefore, has many different facets.

Euronews: Zaporizhzhia is only 20 kilometres from the front line. Russia is now even attacking city buses with drones. How has the situation in Zaporizhzhia changed in recent weeks?

Kharchenko: As far as public transport is concerned, the past week has been more or less calm. But we know that the enemy is insidious, and since the beginning of the year, we have seen systematic attacks on public transport.

Among other things, we have discussed here whether our municipal transport operator can receive vehicles as a form of humanitarian aid. We ourselves are providing additional protection: anti-drone tunnels and anti-drone nets in key locations in certain neighbourhoods, and shatterproof film on the vehicles so that people are not injured by fragments.

Everything we can do at the municipal level, we are of course doing. On this occasion, however, I would like to thank the Ukrainian defence forces, because they are doing incredible things. Countless attacks, countless drones, missiles and Shaheds are being repelled. Only thanks to their superhuman work can we lead a more or less normal life.

Euronews: Ukraine is facing its fourth winter of war. Putin wants to attack infrastructure even harder this winter, as the Financial Times has reported. How do you see the coming months?

Kharchenko: We constantly see that war is being waged by attacking critical infrastructure. These attacks are terrorism and terror against the peaceful civilian population. Perhaps this is part of the Russian strategy to break Ukraine and show that they can take everything from us, basic living conditions, amenities, and comfort.

But the city is preparing. We are actively reinforcing critical infrastructure and protecting the most important facilities: substations, heating plants and pumping stations. I would like to take this opportunity to thank all my teams who are actively working on this. But we understand that the enemy is insidious and that we do not know the scale of the attacks. That is why we do what we can and keep going.

Euronews: A few days ago, the power supply to the nuclear power plant in Zaporizhzhia was cut again. How are the residents of Zaporizhzhia coping with the constant threat posed by the plant?

Kharchenko: This is of course a tragedy. We very much hope that even in the terrorist state of Russia, there is still some remnant of common sense. Because to play with attacks on such facilities means destroying people in the 21st century and deliberately doing everything to ensure that the peaceful civilian population dies. We are very much hoping for a response from all the countries of the European Union, the United States and all responsible politicians, so that they prevent this catastrophe in Ukraine, especially as it would unfold in the immediate vicinity of Zaporizhzhia.

Euronews: Financial aid for Ukraine is currently being debated a great deal and very controversially. What do you want from the European Union and from Germany? And what do you say to people who do not want to support Ukraine?

Kharchenko: I would like to say that Ukraine is currently fighting for values that are taken for granted in Europe: human life, freedom, freedom of choice, state sovereignty. These are things that are the norm in the European Union. But unfortunately, Ukraine is now simply fighting to continue to exist on the world map. And every Ukrainian knows that their state is in great danger.

First of all, I would like to thank you for all the help that has been provided to Ukraine, to our municipalities and especially to Zaporizhzhia. And of course, I hope that this support will in no way diminish and that there will be more projects to provide military equipment for Ukraine. Because even if we achieve a just peace and, as part of negotiations and all the political processes under way, there is a ceasefire, Ukraine must remain strong and resilient, with its own effective defence forces, so that this war is never repeated.

Euronews: What would a possible ceasefire along the current front line mean for Zaporizhzhia?

Kharchenko: It is a constant life in fear. Twenty kilometres is a very short distance, and the enemy attacks incredibly often. We hope that people will simply be able to live normally again if there is an agreement on a temporary ceasefire or some kind of de-escalation. At the same time, we know that we must still remain very strong, institutionally strong and strong in terms of infrastructure. And we still have to protect our city.

Euronews: Would it be acceptable for you to cede the areas currently occupied by Russia if, in return, there were peace?

Kharchenko: To be honest, I do not have the expertise to give a well-founded answer to that. This is not really my level of responsibility; it is more at the national level. I am more concerned with life in my municipality and with what Zaporizhzhia needs.

Euronews: Is there anything else you would like to say?

Kharchenko: I would like to thank the Konrad Adenauer Foundation for giving us the opportunity to be here today, to talk about Zaporizhzhia and the actual situation, about how difficult it is to live in a war, and of course to share our experiences. I would also like to thank all the partners who are helping us, our partner cities Oberhausen and Magdeburg in Germany and especially THW (editor's note: Federal Agency for Technical Relief) and GIZ (editor's note: German Agency for International Cooperation), which are providing us with huge support by supplying equipment and special vehicles for our municipal services.

După ce PressOne a arătat cum timp de aproape 13 ani niciun director al Serviciului Român de Informații (SRI) nu a prezentat în plenul Parlamentului rapoartele anuale de activitate ale instituției, așa cum îi cere lege, Ilie Bolojan și Ludovic Orban au susținut că PNL nu se opune dezbaterii acestora în Parlament.

Nouă rapoarte au trecut prin Parlament fără să fie prezentate și dezbătute efectiv, iar alte cinci, din perioada 2021–2025, sunt în continuare blocate la Birourile Permanente Reunite ale Camerei Deputaților și Senatului. Situația este documentată într-o investigație publicată de PressOne, semnată de Ionuț Dumitrescu și Emilia Șercan, care arată cum controlul parlamentar asupra SRI a ajuns să fie exercitat mai degrabă formal.

Întrebați miercuri, 11 noiembrie, despre rapoartele restante, Ilie Bolojan și Ludovic Orban au susținut că PNL nu se opune dezbaterii acestora în Parlament.

„Consider că toate rapoartele care sunt prevăzute în legislație trebuie să fie dezbătute, prezentate și publicate. Și PNL nu va bloca, nu va amâna și nu va tergiversa aceste lucruri”, a declarat Ilie Bolojan. 

La rândul său, Ludovic Orban, președinte al Camerei Deputaților în mai 2021 când în plenul Parlamentului au fost prezentate simultan cinci co-rapoarte și cinci rapoarte de activitate ale Comisiei SRI, fără a fi prezentate însă și cele cinci rapoarte de activitate ale SRI aferente intervalului 2015 - 2019, a atribuit întârzierile PSD.

Acesta a susținut că o situație similară exista și atunci când a preluat conducerea Camerei Deputaților și că PNL sprijină dezbaterea rapoartelor SRI.

PressOne a discutat cu Marian Zulean, profesor abilitat la Universitatea din București și specialist în studii de securitate, despre gravitatea situației documentate în investigație, responsabilitatea parlamentarilor și schimbările necesare pentru ca instituțiile statului să exercite un control real asupra serviciilor de informații.

„Parlamentarii au principala parte de vină”

Investigația PressOne aduce date concrete despre modul în care funcționează controlul parlamentar asupra SRI, spune Marian Zulean, informații pe care acesta nu le-a avut până acum la dispoziție, deși studiază de mai mulți ani domeniul securității, adaugă el. 

„S-a aprins lumina în cămară pe tema controlului parlamentar asupra Serviciului Român de Informații”, spune profesorul, care consideră că investigația a atins „o temă foarte fierbinte”.

În opinia sa, faptul că directorii serviciului nu au mai prezentat rapoartele anuale în Parlament reprezintă „o sfidare a mecanismelor democratice”. Responsabilitatea nu aparține, însă, exclusiv conducerii SRI.

„Parlamentarii au principala parte de vină. Nu știm de ce ordin: teamă sau poate funcționează suspiciunea că, la rândul lor, controlorii sunt controlați. Nu știu răspunsul la asta, dar e clar că este o sfidare a mecanismelor democratice”, explică Zulean.

Profesorul amintește că România a fost nevoită să demonstreze că dispune de mecanisme de control democratic asupra serviciilor de informații înainte de aderarea la NATO și Uniunea Europeană. Consideră, totuși, că standardele atinse la momentul respectiv au fost mai degrabă minimale.

„Am intrat, să zicem, cu nota cinci. Adică am trecut pragul”, subliniază expertul.

După aderare, spune Zulean, au lipsit evaluările bazate pe date concrete care să arate cum funcționează, în practică, aceste mecanisme.

Ce nu mai află Parlamentul despre activitatea SRI

Lipsa dezbaterilor parlamentare înseamnă, potrivit lui Marian Zulean, și pierderea unei ocazii de a verifica în ce măsură SRI își îndeplinește principalele misiuni, de la combaterea terorismului și contraspionaj până la securitatea cibernetică.

ISJ Maramureș face verificări după ce Cătălin Cherecheș, condamnat pentru corupție, le-a vorbit elevilor unei școli din Baia Mare. Copiii l-au mai întâlnit pe fostul edil și în anii trecuți

Postările publice consultate de PressOne arată că Maria Chira are legături mai vechi cu familia Cherecheș, iar elevii aceleiași școli au participat și în alți ani la întâlniri cu fostul primar, organizate la sediul administrației locale.

AUDIO. Marele simulacru al controlului parlamentar. (I) Nouă rapoarte anuale de activitate ale SRI, aprobate de Parlament fără dezbatere. Din 2013, Directorul SRI nu a mai dat socoteală în fața aleșilor

PressOne dezvăluie, într-o serie de investigații, etapele și momentele care au slăbit sistematic controlul democratic asupra SRI, dar și cine sunt politicienii care au ținut cea mai mare structură de informații din România departe de ochii publicului. Astăzi, primul episod.

Profesorul susține că românii trebuie să afle în ce măsură SRI și-a îndeplinit misiunile de bază, pentru care primește bani de la bugetul de stat.

Dezbaterile ar trebui să le ofere parlamentarilor posibilitatea de a cere explicații și despre alte aspecte ale activității SRI, asupra cărora există încă multe întrebări.

„Nu știm dacă suntem ascultați prin acele mandate de siguranță națională, cum sunt selectați liderii, dacă există ofițeri acoperiți sau firme private ale serviciului care distorsionează piața”, spune Zulean, care adaugă că dezbaterea rapoartelor SRI ar trebui să aibă loc în plenul Parlamentului, unde toți aleșii ar putea pune întrebări despre activitatea serviciului, nu doar membrii comisiei de control.

„Mecanismul de control democratic civil nu este o fiță. În orice democrație, puterea e a poporului, ea este delegată prin alegeri parlamentarilor și tocmai de aceea Parlamentul este principalul mecanism de control”. 

Avem legi și comisii. Dar funcționează?

Marian Zulean consideră că problemele controlului parlamentar asupra SRI sunt legate și de legislația învechită. Legea siguranței naționale datează din 1991, când securitatea cibernetică nici măcar nu reprezenta o preocupare. De atunci, mai multe administrații prezidențiale, de la Emil Constantinescu la Klaus Iohannis, au încercat să actualizeze legislația, fără succes.

„Cineva, așa, speculativ, poate spune că tocmai serviciilor de informații le convine legislația asta învechită”, spune Zulean.

În ceea ce privește soluțiile, profesorul este preocupat în special de pregătirea celor care au responsabilitatea de a supraveghea serviciile de informații.

„Cel mai mult și mai mult mă îngrijorează modalitatea în care sunt educați controlorii, acel mecanism cu colegiile naționale de apărare, de siguranță, unde nu știm dacă nu sunt mai degrabă selectați yesmeni și oamenii lor, și nu adevărați reprezentanți ai poporului, care sunt intruzivi, care verifică în amănunt”. 

Pe termen scurt, Zulean consideră că trebuie schimbat modul în care sunt pregătiți cei care exercită controlul parlamentar. Pentru o reformă mai amplă este nevoie și de voință politică. 

„Legea de organizare a SRI spune că serviciul se află sub control parlamentar. Dar, dacă ne uităm un paragraf mai sus, vedem că SRI se află și sub îndrumarea și controlul CSAT. Deci, președintele, împreună cu Parlamentul, ar putea să formeze o comisie pentru reforma sistemului de securitate”.

Universitatea Politehnică de Nord-Vest din China a achiziționat luna trecută două cipuri H200, pentru 123 de mii de dolari, în ciuda faptului că se află pe lista neagră a SUA, potrivit documentelor de achiziție din 21 octombrie de pe site-ul său, consultate de Reuters. Universitatea chineză a mai a achiziționat, în acest an, cipuri H200 și alte procesoare Nvidia avansate, destinate inteligenței artificiale, prin intermediul a cinci contracte de închiriere a capacității de calcul de la companii chineze. 

H200 este unul dintre cele mai puternice cipuri Nvidia destinate inteligenței artificiale. Aceste procesoare sunt folosite pentru antrenarea și rularea unor modele AI complexe, care necesită capacități foarte mari de calcul. Tehnologia poate avea însă și aplicații militare, de la analiza informațiilor și proiectarea armamentului până la dezvoltarea unor sisteme avansate pentru armată. 

Pentru ca acestea să fie exportate, Nvidia trebuie să aibă aprobarea din partea SUA. De regulă, acestea sunt refuzate în cazul instituțiilor incluse pe lista neagră, precum universitatea menționată anterior, potrivit Reuters. SUA a adăugat-o pe lista sa neagră comercială (denumită “Entity List”) în 2001, din cauza presupusei sale implicări în activități de proliferare a rachetelor și în cercetare militară. În 2019, departamentul a înăsprit restricțiile, stabilind ca licențele pentru exportul de tehnologie americană supusă controlului către universitate să fie, în majoritatea cazurilor, respinse.

Universitatea Politehnică de Nord-Vest face parte din grupul “Seven Sons of National Defense” (“Cei Șapte Fii ai Apărării Naționale”), care se află pe lista sancțiunilor impuse de SUA, fiind o rețea de instituții de învățământ superior din China care desfășoară cercetări în domenii precum aviația militară, rachete și sateliți. Cipurile au fost cumpărate pentru facultatea de management prin intermediul unei companii chineze, Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology, și nu direct de la Nvidia. 

Investigația Reuters arată că fenomenul nu se limitează la această universitate. Agenția a identificat 26 de documente de achiziții și contracte comerciale din acest an care indică faptul că universități și institute de cercetare din China au cumpărat procesoare Nvidia supuse restricțiilor americane sau au închiriat capacitate de calcul bazată pe acestea. 

Printre instituțiile de învățământ menționate se numără și Universitatea Shenzhen, care a cumpărat trei cipuri H100, și Universitatea de Tehnologie Wuhan, care a achiziționat un server cu un cip H100 și alte patru cipuri A100. De asemenea, Universitatea Beihang, o altă instituție din grupul “Seven Sons of National Defense”, ce are legături strânse cu industria aerospațială și de apărare a Chinei, a cumpărat patru cipuri A800.

Procesoarele ajung la aceste instituții prin intermediul unor furnizori locali, care cumpără cipurile sau oferă acces la servere echipate cu acestea. Documentele nu precizează întotdeauna de unde provin procesoarele și unde sunt amplasate serverele. 

Dezvăluirile au loc într-un moment în care Nvidia și directorul său general, Jensen Huang, se confruntă cu o presiune tot mai mare la Washington, pentru lobby-ul său în favoarea unor restricții mai relaxate privind vânzările de cipuri de inteligență artificială către China, în urma unor rapoarte care susțin că ar fi fost vizat de o operațiune de spionaj chineză. 

Huang susține că menținerea vânzărilor către China ar proteja poziția de lider tehnologic a SUA și ar păstra dependența clienților chinezi de tehnologia americană. În schimb, unii oficiali americani avertizează că accesul Chinei la aceste cipuri ar putea accelera dezvoltarea sistemelor AI utilizate pentru proiectarea armelor, analiza informațiilor și modernizarea armatei. Huang este acum și în centrul altui scandal, după ce s-a aflat că și-ar fi înșelat soția cu o spioană din China. 

Atât democrații, cât și republicanii din Congres au solicitat măsuri de control mai stricte asupra accesului Chinei la cipuri avansate de inteligență artificială, cum ar fi urmărirea comenzilor de cipuri și o supraveghere mai strictă a exporturilor din partea Congresului.

The island nation's highest court overturned a 1986 law criminalising consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex.

A decade-long legal battle led by LGBT+ Trinidadian activists successfully ended as Trinidad and Tobago's highest court overturned a long-running law criminalising gay sex.

The UK-based final court of appeal for British dependencies and overseas territories issued a unanimous decision Tuesday that the 1986 Sexual Offences Act could not be used to prosecute private, consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex.

Seen as a landmark ruling for LGBT+ rights in the Caribbean, this law had previously carried sentences of two years for "serious indecency" and five years for "buggery".

"What I'm going to be doing in the coming months is very targeted activism about how the Caribbean, not just Trinidad and Tobago, deals with endemic homophobia," said LGBT+ Trinidadian activist Jason Jones after the verdict was read.

'Phenomenal victory for gay rights'

Freedom Law Chambers, the law firm that represented Jones, said in a statement that the judgement represented a "phenomenal victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, which issued the decision, said constitutional rights must be interpreted in a way that makes them "practical and effective in the present day, not in the past."

The judgement was welcomed by UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk, who called it a significant milestone for rights and equality.

"I hope the judgment will help remove a longstanding source of stigma, exclusion, barriers and violence experienced by Trinidadians and Tobagonians based on sexual orientation and gender identity," Turk said.

Sandu îi amintește președintului că există cel puțin două hotărâri judecătorești care dovedesc abuzuri ale Inspecției Judiciare și ale CSM împotriva unor magistrați: a indicat între altele decizia Curții Europene a Drepturilor Omului în cazul fostului judecător Cristi Danileț, sancționat pe nedrept, și hotărârea Curții de Justiție a Uniunii, care critică practica prescripțiilor în România.

După ce s-a eschivat la intrebările pe subiecte grele, Nicușor Dan a mers mai departe și a anunțat o măsură fără precendent. Întrebat despre o evidentă incompatibilitate care o implică pe actuala șefă a Parchetului General, Cristina Chiriac (pe care de altfel șeful statului a numit-o și a lăudat-o public în mai multe rânduri) l-a anunțat pe jurnalistul care a adresat-o – Ovidiu Vanghele de la Centrul de Investigații Media – că nu mai are ce căuta în conferințele de presă de la Cotroceni.

Pe scurt: Ovidiu Vanghele a dezvăluit recent cum Cristina Chiriac ar fi încălcat independența procurorilor. Printr-o cerere de mutare intempestivă (aprobată de Curtea Supremă) a unui proces de la o curte de apel la alta. Subalternii săi refuzaseră pe rând blocarea procesului de la Craiova, așa că procurorul general a considerat că e nevoie să facă ea însăși cererea de strămutare la Înalta Curte.

O parte din secția pentru procurori din Consiliul Magistraturii ar fi vrut verificări suplimentare, însă 4 membri au decis că nu se impune o anchetă. Însăși Cristina Chiriac a votat împotriva acțiunii ce o viza direct. Să mai spunem că, dincolo de prevederile din legislația națională care interzic în mod explicit excluderea unui jurnalist de la evenimentele publice ale unei instituții, mai multe decizii ale CEDO toarnă apă rece peste supărarea președintelui: ele spun că libertatea de exprimare acoperă și ideile care șochează sau ofensează și că politicenii sunt obligați să accepte un grad de critică mai ridicat decât restul cetățenilor.

De asemenea, jurnaliștilor li se permit libertăți mai largi de exprimare (chiar și „exagerări”), atâta timp cât expun fapte de interes public.

După anunțul legat de ridicarea acreditării lui Ovidiu Vanghele, câteva ONG-uri au decis să boicoteze o întâlnire  pe care o aveau astăzi cu președintele.

Că Inspecția Judiciară și CSM funcționează totuși „brici” ne asigură și ministrul PSD al Justiției – Radu Marinescu.

Austeritatea, singura constantă

Dacă în ceea ce privește justiția, viața politică și influența serviciilor secrete în societate răspunsurile lui Nicușor Dan au fost pline de jumătăți de adevăr, o certitudine s-a desprins în mod clar din conferința-maraton de ieri: măsurile de reducere a deficitului bugetar vor continua și – foarte probabil – ele vor presupune noi tăieri în instituțiile și în companiile de stat.

Președintele a pornit de la constatarea că, din deficitul ajuns la 150 de miliarde de lei, aproape jumătate înseamnă doar dobînzile pe care România le-a acumulat deja. Bucureștiul se împrumută de mai multă vreme doar pentru a menține pe linia de plutire instituțiile și serviciile publice esențiale.

Prima grijă a președintelui, deci, pare să fie menținerea încrederii investitorilor și a agențiilor de evaluare financiară. În caz contrar, a spus el, Bucureștiul ar fi obligat să încheie un nou acord cu FMI, care ar presupune măsuri cu mult mai dure decît cele de pînă acum.

Sub amenințarea – deocamdată teoretică – a unui program de austeritate gestionat de Fondul Monetar Internațional, care ar fi locurile din care Guvernul dominat de PSD ar mai putea să taie?

SRI, scăpat de sub control

Serviciul Român de Informații nu mai dă socoteală nimănui: nici cetățenilor și nici Parlamentului deja de ani buni – arată o investigație PressOne. Nouă rapoarte de activitate ale SRI au fost aprobate de Parlament fără dezbaterea prevăzută de legea, iar din anul 2013 directorul instituției nu s-a mai prezentat în plen pentru a prezenta rapoartele anuale de activitate și a lămuri controversele care planează în societate asupra serviciului.

Printre aceste rapoarte se numără și cel din 2024, an în care SRI a furnizat președintelui României una dintre cele patru „note de informare” în baza cărora Curtea Constituțională a României a decis anularea primului tur al alegerilor prezidențiale.

Într-un răspuns pentru site-ul PressOne, cel mai mare serviciu de informații din România, care are un buget consistent și un număr necunoscut de angajați, a încercat să inducă în mod fals ideea că cele nouă rapoarte au fost prezentate și dezbătute în legislativ, deși toate dovezile arată că acest lucru nu s-a întâmplat.

Investigația semnată de Ionuț Dumitrescu și Emilia Șercan arată și cine sunt politicienii care au ținut SRI departe de ochii publicului.

Șeful Senatului, penelistul Mircea Abrudean, a declarat că îl va invita pe directorul interimar al SRI, generalul Răzvan Ionescu, să prezinte rapoartele, dar că datoria lui se încheie odată cu trimiterea documentelor către Parlament. Invitarea directorului în plen ar depinde de Birourile Permanente Unite, spune acesta, însă tot președinții celor două camere conduc și BPN-urile și stabilesc ordinea de zi.

Sorin Grindeanu nu a răspuns apelurilor și mesajelor jurnaliștilor. Într-o declarație de anul trecut, acesta spunea că rapoartele SRI vor fi puse pe ordinea de zi a plenului abia după ce va fi numit un nou director.

Întrebați de reporterul Știrilor Recorder David Bularca despre blocarea rapoartelor SRI, președintele PNL Ilie Bolojan și Ludovic Orban, proaspăr revenit în partid, au dat vina pe social-democrați.

Să mai spunem că președintele Nicușor Dan a promis numirea unui nou director la SRI toată campania electorală pentru prezidențiale. După ce a ajuns la Palatul Cotroceni a tot amânat termenul pentru numirea de noi șefi la toate serviciile secrete – nu doar la SRI – până în punctul în care a ajuns să declare vara aceasta că subiectul nu mai reprezintă o chestiune atât de urgentă.

Aseară a spus că va face numiri în momentul în care va exista o majoritate parlamentară în acest sens. Serviciul Român de Informații nu mai are un director civil plin din 3 iulie 2023

The European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act would introduce new protections against unfair online commercial practices, alongside a separate enforcement reform that could see companies fined up to 6% of their annual global turnover.

From online subscriptions that are difficult to cancel to social media features designed to keep users scrolling, the EU says it wants to make the digital economy fairer for consumers.

The European Commission unveiled its proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) on Wednesday, setting out new rules to tackle manipulative online practices, improve price transparency and strengthen protections for children.

“We are tackling the new unfair commercial practices that distort consumers' choices and put pressure on them, undermining their ability to make informed choices,” said executive vice-president and EU tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen.

Among the measures presented in Brussels on Wednesday are a ban on manipulative marketing tactics, known as ‘dark patterns’; requirements for clear and transparent pricing; fairness by design for digital platforms and services; the option for consumers to disable addictive design features; and new rules for influencer marketing.

A revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation was presented alongside the DFA. It aims to grant the Commission stronger powers to investigate and issue fines directly in large-scale cases affecting consumers across multiple countries, such as the recently launched action against video game companies including Activision Blizzard.

“The Digital Fairness Act, together with the update to the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation, represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years,” said EU consumer protection commissioner Michael McGrath.

The proposals are the latest in a patchwork of EU laws being put forward in Brussels to regulate e-commerce and online consumer protection. They are also part of a wider push to rein in Big Tech companies.

The DFA would work alongside the recently proposed EU Kids Act, which aims to shift responsibility for protecting children online towards companies.

It would also complement the Digital Services Act and Digital Markets Act, which seek to make the online world safer, fairer and more transparent, as well as the AI Act, which governs the use of artificial intelligence.

Enforcement

The proposed revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation would give the European Commission direct powers to investigate large-scale cases with a major impact on consumers across multiple EU countries.

It would also speed up and improve coordination between national consumer authorities in cross-border cases, setting deadlines for key steps and improving how penalties are coordinated, for example when fines are collected in different jurisdictions.

Companies found to have violated consumer protection rules in these large-scale cases could face fines of up to 6% of their annual global turnover. The DMA already allows for fines of up to 10%, while the DSA provides for fines of up to 6%.

This approach has had mixed results in the EU. While some cases, such as Apple's €500 million fine in April last year, have brought about changes to its App Store policies, others, such as Google's antitrust cases, have had more limited results in changing behaviour.

Crucially for Big Tech, non-EU companies would be required to appoint a legal representative in the EU to cooperate with national authorities and the Commission.

Stronger consumer protections

The DFA introduces several proposed protections for consumers online, including a ban on ‘dark patterns’ – such as fake claims that a product is almost sold out to pressure consumers into making a purchase.

Consumers would be given the option to disable addictive design features such as endless scrolling and autoplay videos.

Pricing must be communicated clearly and transparently. This applies in several areas, including dynamic pricing for tickets to sporting or cultural events, where prices must be displayed in real time to show consumers what they may have to pay.

The rules also cover virtual currencies, where conversion rates are not always clear. This can be an issue on platforms such as video games, where players make purchases using in-game currency rather than real money.

The DFA would also restrict practices that encourage children to overspend in video games, including gambling-simulating loot boxes and mechanisms that pressure them to pay to progress.

Examples include wheels of fortune features such as FIFA Ultimate Team packs. The proposed restrictions would not apply in the same way to adult gamers, for whom loot boxes and streak mechanics would remain permitted.

Online subscriptions and contracts must also be easier to cancel. Consumers would receive reminders before free trials turn into paid subscriptions, while automatic renewals would require a conscious choice rather than being a forgotten obligation.

Online consumers would also be able to reach a human being in customer service rather than being left with a chatbot.

The DFA also proposes rules for influencers for the first time, requiring content creators to disclose commercial content and preventing them from exploiting children's trust.

It would also ban unfair personalised advertising and pricing that targets minors or exploits people's vulnerabilities.

“The DFA will make sure the digital economy works for consumers, not against them,” said McGrath. “Businesses that play by the rules should not lose out to those that cut corners.”

The Commission's impact assessment estimates that the rules would spare consumers €88.4 billion in financial losses between 2025 and 2035.

Including time lost to unfair practices, it puts the annual benefit at €13.7 billion, against recurring costs to businesses of €678 million a year, once overlaps between measures are accounted for.

Response

Tech leaders have cautiously welcomed the new rules, but some have raised concerns about mixed messages from Brussels.

While EU leaders have called for simpler rules across economic sectors since the European elections in 2024, this year has seen a glut of proposals, particularly concerning online platforms and services, raising concerns about potential overlap.

Isabelle Roccia, Managing Director for IAPP in Europe, told Euronews Next: “The rationale to update rules, some created 20 years ago, to digital economy makes sense, but there are rules already in place across consumer protection, privacy, platform regulation, AI, etc.

“Is the DFA introducing new tools that organisations, consumers and regulators don’t already have in their toolbox? Does it embrace the Commission’s simplification objective or unduly add to the complexity of online governance?”

Others feel the proposal is a good start, but that the devil will be in the detail.

Monika Zdzieborska, counsel in Clifford Chance's Tech/Digital practice, told Euronews Next: “The debate is likely to centre on three fault lines. The first is coherence: does the DFA fill genuine gaps, or does it add another layer on top of the DSA, AI Act, GDPR and Kids Act?

“The second is defaults: should consumers have to switch off features designed to keep them engaged, or should those features be off from the start?

“The third is proportionality: should a shopping site, a streaming service, a game and a social network be regulated in the same way, or should the law reflect their very different risks?

“With the Kids Act on a parallel track, the two files will be negotiated side by side. Decisions on one, particularly on minors, addictive design and age checks, are likely to influence the other.”

On consumer rights, Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, policy officer at European Digital Rights (EDRi), told Euronews that the organisation was concerned that the proposal’s rules on addictive design still relied too heavily on individuals finding the off switch, rather than requiring companies to prevent harmful practices.

“The Commission has spent years studying how companies manipulate us online. Now comes the uncomfortable part: telling those companies to stop. Parliament and Member States have plenty of work ahead to give this law the teeth it deserves.”

The proposal must now be examined by MEPs and national governments before passing into European law.

She has also been under EU sanctions since September.

“Xenia Fedorova has notably presented Western and European support for Ukraine as a factor prolonging the war, has described Russia as a country seeking peace while portraying Europe as advocating confrontation, has challenged established facts relating to the illegal transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children, and has disseminated messages depicting European and NATO policies as threats to European security”, the document states.

A Swedish company announced a partnership with Portuguese industrial group Vangest to produce eight complex parts in Portugal for Gripen E/F fighters. The Swedish jet is among the options to renew the Portuguese Air Force's F-16 fleet.

The Portuguese industrial group Vangest, best known for moulds and plastic parts for various sectors and which has been expanding in the aerospace sector, is going to produce components for Saab's Gripen fighter jets.

In a statement, the company explains that the "partnership is part of Saab's work to expand its international manufacturing network and strengthen the production capacity of the Gripen E/F".

The agreement covers the production of eight complex components for Gripen E/F fighter jets at the group's facilities in Marinha Grande, north of Lisbon, and is expected to create "new skilled jobs" in the region.

The Swedish company justifies the partnership with Vangest's "advanced manufacturing capabilities and experience", in an alliance that also has the potential for "expansion in the coming years".

"With Vangest, we are expanding our manufacturing network and strengthening production capacity, while at the same time giving Portuguese industry a concrete role in the Gripen programme," said Johan Segertoft, head of Saab's Gripen business unit, quoted in the company's statement, stressing how the cooperation reaffirms Saab's commitment "to the development of Portugal's aerospace industry".

The value of the deal, including the investment involved, the number of components to be produced or realistic estimates of the number of jobs created, was not specified, nor was the start date for production.

The announcement comes at a time when the launch of the process to renew the Portuguese Air Force's F-16s is awaited. The Gripen fighters are one of the fighter jet models mentioned as a possible purchase option for the Portuguese government.

In Wednesday's statement, the Swedish company says that the selection of its model "would offer more opportunities" to deepen the cooperation now announced, aiming at the "development of Portugal's aerospace and defence industry and strengthening its role in the European defence industrial landscape".

Horseback wrestling, endurance racing, archery and traditional games grew from the skills of nomadic life. At the World Nomad Games, those traditions now draw athletes from more than 100 countries.

When the sixth World Nomad Games were held in Kyrgyzstan in September 2026, many visitors and journalists were struck by the scale of the event.

What began in Kyrgyzstan in 2014 as an effort to revive and promote nomadic sports and traditions has grown into a global event. More than 3,000 athletes from 109 countries took part in the 2026 Games, competing in 43 sports.

Participants came from across the world, including many countries with no direct connection to nomadic culture. What began as a regional cultural initiative has developed into a major international sporting event.

So, what are the skills that have attracted such widespread interest?

Historically shaped by battlefield training, hunting and the demands of nomadic life, these skills helped develop strength, endurance, agility and horsemanship. Today they are sports, but for peoples with strong nomadic traditions, including Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Uzbeks, Turkmens, Tajiks and Mongols, they also remain expressions of history, identity and cultural continuity.

Historical accounts describe wrestling, archery and horsemanship as important parts of warrior training and social gatherings across the steppe. These traditions have survived for generations.

“Just as every nation has its own national games, our equestrian and national sports can be called the soul of the Kazakh people. Of course, in a developing world, riding horses and shooting arrows might seem unusual or like something from the past to some people, but for us, national sports are our wealth,” said Baurzhan Mugyzharov, trainer of Kazakhstan’s kokpar team.

There are many different nomadic games. Athletes at the 2026 World Nomad Games competed in 43 sports, but those demanding endurance and strength from both horse and rider often attract some of the greatest public interest.

Kazakh nomadic culture is closely associated with horses. Equestrian games remain popular and are often part of social events and celebrations.

Among the best known is kokpar, described in the 19th century by American diplomat Eugene Schuyler as a game in which “one man holds a kid thrown over his saddle and everyone else tries to tear it from him.”

In modern competition, four riders from each team are on the field at a time. Players try to pick up a dummy carcass from the ground while riding and carry it towards a designated scoring circle.

The game demands strength and agility from both horse and rider. The dummy used in competition weighs around 30 to 33 kilograms.

Kokpar is part of Kazakh tradition and has an equivalent in Kyrgyzstan known as kok boru. Thousands of spectators travelled from Kazakhstan to watch the kokpar finals at the World Nomad Games in Kyrgyzstan, while many young Kazakhs continue to take up the sport.

“Kazakhs have a tradition of getting children onto horses from a very tender age. Once they grow up enough to hold the reins properly, they are made to race in competitions and play kokpar. We guide each child according to their aptitude, because this is our national sport and a tradition handed down from our ancestors,” Mugyzharov said.

Traditional horse racing in Central Asia often places greater emphasis on stamina than short-distance speed.

At the 2026 World Nomad Games, long-distance races included a 25-kilometre event, while a separate 300-kilometre endurance marathon was held over three days.

Horsemanship also forms the basis of other traditional sports.

Audaryspak, or horseback wrestling, is one of the clearest examples of how skills once associated with mounted warriors developed into organised competition. Two riders try to unseat each other from the saddle, gripping, pushing and pulling while controlling their horses at the same time.

“At the recent World Nomad Games, which brought together representatives from many countries, we saw significant progress in the development of audaryspak in Kazakhstan. Here in Kazakhstan, national championships are held systematically for youth, juniors and adults. The results speak for themselves. At the competition held in Issyk-Kul, Kyrgyzstan, four of our six Kazakh wrestlers won gold medals, one won silver and one won bronze. As a result, Kazakhstan took first place in the team standings,” said Zhanbatyr Bekmusaev, Vice-Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Audaryspak Association.

Wrestling is also among the most popular non-equestrian traditional sports. Several Central Asian nations have developed their own forms, each with distinctive rules, clothing and rituals.

In Mongolian bökh, wrestlers wear traditional clothing known as zodog and shuudag and perform a ritual dance before competing. A wrestler loses when any part of the body above the knee touches the ground.

Kazakh kuresi is fought standing, with competitors wearing special jackets and trying to throw their opponent onto their back or shoulders.

Uzbek kurash is also fought standing. Ground wrestling and grips below the waist are prohibited, with competitors relying on throws and sweeps to defeat their opponent.

For those who prefer precision to strength, there is archery.

Traditional archery takes several forms, including disciplines practised on horseback. In Kazakhstan, horseback archery reflects techniques associated with mounted warriors who needed to shoot while moving at speed.

“In our Kazakh tradition, our ancestors used to shoot while riding on horseback. That's why, when shooting from horseback, the arrows need to stay in place and not move around. So we shoot differently from Europeans. They used long bows from the ground and pulled the string with three fingers. Horsemen could accidentally release that pinch so we are using our thumbs to pull. On the thumb, there’s a thumb ring. The rings can be made of leather, wood or brass,” explained Nurzhan Zhaksylikuly, an archer from Kazakhstan’s Zhetysu region.

There are also traditional games that require less physical strength but remain closely linked to nomadic life.

In Zhetysu, known as the region of the seven rivers, schools teach young boys and girls games such as asyk and bes asyk.

Asyk is a traditional game played with sheep knuckle bones. Players use one bone to knock others from a marked area, with accuracy and control determining the winner.

“Asyk is a traditional heritage left to us by our ancestors. It is played by everyone, from five-year-old children to the elderly. This is our national game. Speaking of its benefits, asyk fosters flexibility, agility and accuracy,” said Zhetysu regional team trainer Ashat Turlybekov.

“If we look at the recent championship held in Kyrgyzstan, we can see that games like asyk atu and bestas are developing actively,” Turlybekov said, adding that the games also have practical benefits.

“Instead of children sitting on their phones, it is much better for them to learn useful skills like precision, agility and marksmanship. In a single game, each child is given five to seven minutes. Moving back and forth gives the child strength and energy.”

There is also a Mongolian competition in which participants break animal vertebrae with their bare hands, another example of how demonstrations of physical strength have developed into organised contests.

Governments and sporting organisations across the region continue to invest in traditional sports. Many have dedicated federations, schools and championships aimed at widening participation and passing skills on to younger generations.

International interest is also growing. The presence of athletes from more than 100 countries at the World Nomad Games has given these sports a new role in tourism and cultural promotion far beyond the communities where they originated.

For nomadic cultures, however, their revival is about more than international attention.

“We are reviving our history and bringing forgotten heritage back to light,” said Erlan Ashym, founder of an equestrian club in Karaganda.

For Ashym, developing national sports is also a way of strengthening cultural identity and reconnecting younger generations with traditions associated with horses and the steppe.

“Ultimately, our main goal isn't just to promote sports; it is to restore our core national identity through the strength of our history, traditions, national sports and the horse.”

From ancient Silk Road cities and magnificent architecture to vibrant bazaars and rich traditions, join Lilly Douse as she discovers the history, culture and flavours of Uzbekistan.

Uzbekistan is a country shaped by centuries of history, where ancient Silk Road cities, magnificent architecture and rich cultural traditions come together. From the bustling streets of Tashkent to the historic treasures of Samarkand, it offers a fascinating insight into Central Asia.

In this episode of Grand Voyager, Lilly begins her journey in the capital, Tashkent, visiting the Islamic Civilization Centre to discover the country's religious, cultural and historical heritage. Food is another important part of Uzbek culture. At the Museum of Plov, Lilly discovers the story behind one of the country's most celebrated traditional dishes, learning about its preparation and significance in Uzbek hospitality.

From Tashkent, Lilly travels to Samarkand, one of the most important cities along the ancient Silk Road. At Registan Square she meets with Khurshid Narimov, from Akasha Travel to take in the spectacular madrasahs, renowned for their intricate tilework and grand architecture, before exploring Shahi-Zinda, a remarkable avenue of historic mausoleums decorated with some of the finest examples of Islamic craftsmanship.

Samarkand is also home to centuries-old artisan traditions. Lilly discovers the ancient art of traditional papermaking, before heading to Siab Bazaar, where the sights, sounds and flavours of local life come together. Finally, she gets hands-on with another Uzbek tradition, learning how to make the country's famous traditional bread.

With its extraordinary architecture, fascinating history, vibrant markets and enduring traditions, Uzbekistan offers a journey through the heart of the Silk Road and a culture that continues to thrive today.

Some travellers are facing issues with their exit from the Schengen zone being missed, leading to the system incorrectly suggesting they have violated the 90 days in any 180-day period rule.

We’ve already covered plenty of stories about the EU’s Entry/Exit System (EES) causing delays at the border over the summer, with some countries easing checks to tackle queues.

Now the UK-based consumer rights publication Which? is warning of another potential problem with the system: Travellers being incorrectly flagged as overstayers.

In case you missed it (those who subscribe to our weekly newsletter certainly won’t have), the EU began rolling out the EES in October 2025, becoming compulsory for 29 countries from 10 April this year.

Replacing passport stamps, the system digitally records entries and exits across all EU countries, excluding Cyprus and Ireland, as well as in Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

It was introduced so that overstayers would be automatically detected. Non-EU citizens can stay for up to 90 days in any 180-day period.

The problem is that some travellers are failing to have their exits recorded, meaning their days in the Schengen zone continue to rack up even after leaving.

As you won’t be directly contacted about your overstay, the issue is often discovered at the border, which is exactly what happened to British writer Jojo Moyes in October.

The Me Before You author had visited Portugal in May, and upon arrival in Marseille she discovered her exit had not been recorded. Officials warned her she could face a €10,000 fine and a two-year ban if she returns before it is fixed.

According to Which?, dozens of readers have been in touch with similar issues.

Euronews Travel has contacted the European Commission for comment.

What to do if you have been incorrectly flagged as overstaying

As we explained in this piece about the “Schengen shuffle”, you can check how many days you have spent in the zone over the past 180 days on the EES website.

If you spot an error in the results – this could be an incorrect number of days, or the system may say it has ‘incomplete data’ – you will need to reach out to the Data Controller for the country in which you believe the error has occurred. The list of Data Controllers is available on the EES website.

In your email, you’ll need to include a passport scan and proof of your exit (i.e. a boarding pass for a flight, or a bus/train ticket) from the Schengen zone.

Vladimir Medinski, negociatorul din partea Federației Ruse, care a participat la negocierile de pace cu SUA și Ucraina la Abu Dhabi, a afirmat că tema centrală a celor două zile de negocieri a fost ideea unui nou cadru de securitate pentru Europa, dar nu a oferit detalii cu privire la conținutul discuțiilor.

Oficialul și-a exprimat, în mod neașteptat, optimismul prudent cu privire la perspectivele ajungerii la un acord pentru încetarea războiului. Într-un interviu acordat agenției de știri ruse Vesti, acesta a fost întrebat dacă țările sunt mai aproape de a ajunge la pace. Medinski a răspuns: “Cred că da. Depinde mult de Ucraina, de poziția Statelor Unite și de faptul dacă Europa își va reveni în fire. În orice caz, toate obiectivele pe care ni le-am stabilit vor fi atinse”. 

În paralel, Moscova a avansat și ideea unor noi acorduri de securitate cu țările europene, inclusiv cu state membre NATO. Alexei Drobinin, un diplomat de rang înalt din Ministerul rus de Externe, a prezentat miercuri mai multe forme posibile de cooperare, inclusiv acorduri bilaterale de neagresiune. Acestea ar presupune angajamentul Rusiei și al unui stat NATO de a nu se ataca reciproc. Drobinin a sugerat că astfel de acorduri ar putea fi însoțite de garanții suplimentare de securitate oferite de Moscova statelor respective.

“Acorduri de acest fel ar putea fi încheiate, printre altele, cu state membre individuale ale NATO, care ar primi apoi, de exemplu, garanții de securitate individuale suplimentare din partea Federației Ruse”, a precizat Drobinin în cadrul conferinței. Cu toate acestea, unii oficiali europeni se opun oricărei discuții privind arhitectura generală de securitate a Europei, afirmând că mai întâi trebuie să fie înregistrate progrese în privința situației Ucrainei – inclusiv un armistițiu – înainte de orice negociere mai amplă privind securitatea continentului, deși oficialii americani au precizat că sunt deschiși la discuții privind această opțiune.

Știrea, în formă inițială. Emisarul american Jared Kushner, care este ginerele lui Donald Trump, a declarat, în cadrul unei conferințe de presă desfășurate în capitala Emiratelor Arabe Unite: “Eu și Steve Witkoff vom călători joi la Moscova pentru a ne întâlni cu președintele Putin, cu scopul de a trece în revistă discuțiile de astăzi și de a încerca să obținem progrese suplimentare în privința unora dintre chestiunile abordate, întrucât observăm acolo anumite deschideri și oportunități”.

În privința reprezentării Europei în negocieri, Kushner a declarat: “Trebuie să-i avem pe europeni la masă. (…) Sper ca mâine, la Moscova, Steve și cu mine să avem succes, iar președintele Putin să-și dea binecuvântarea pentru acest lucru. Cred că, dacă va fi de acord, vom putea înregistra progrese mult mai însemnate în chestiunile care contează cu adevărat”.

Ulterior, cei doi vor zbura la Dublin, unde se vor întâlni cu Volodimir Zelenski “pentru a-l informa cu privire la discuții și a explora mai detaliat unele dintre ideile conturate astăzi”, a mai precizat emisarul.

Totuși, emisarul a afirmat că rușii doresc mai multe progrese înainte de stabilirea unei întâlniri între Putin și Zelenski, precizând că lipsa profundă de încredere între cei doi lideri îngreunează organizarea unei întâlniri. Oficialul a subliniat că aspectele esențiale vizează securitatea postbelică și garanțiile de securitate, precum și evitarea conflictelor și monitorizarea unei eventuale încetări a focului în viitor, dar și că problemele teritoriale vor fi cele mai dificile. 

Separat, Vladimir Medinski, negociatorul din partea Federației Ruse, a afirmat că Rusia și Ucraina au convenit asupra unui schimb de prizonieri de amploare, cel mai recent dintr-o lungă astfel de serie. El a spus și că nu crede că Uniunea Europeană ar trebui să participe la viitoarele discuții.

Le journaliste sportif français Christophe Gleizes a été condamné à sept ans de prison par les autorités algériennes, dans un contexte de tensions entre Paris et Alger.

French football journalist Christophe Gleizes has now spent 500 days behind bars, after he was arrested by Algerian authorities in May 2024 and subsequently handed a seven-year prison sentence.

"Christophe is an ordinary sports journalist, who found himself caught up in a complex diplomatic entanglement that goes far beyond what he had set out to do in Algeria. This is what happens when writing about football becomes punishable by imprisonment", childhood friend Pierre de La Saussay told Euronews.

"His release rests on whether Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune will hand him a pardon", said de La Saussay.

Gleizes, a reporter for French magazines So Foot and Society, was sentenced to seven years in June 2025 for "glorifying terrorism" and possessing "publications intended for propaganda that harms national interests." His conviction was upheld following an appeal that December.

Gleizes' case has drawn widespread condemnation across the sporting community, with prominent figures rallying behind him. Football legend Zinédine Zidane pledged his support, saying he would stand by the journalist "as a parent" during a press conference in July.

Meanwhile, on the eve of the 2026 World Cup, FIFA president Gianni Infantino announced that an empty seat had been reserved for Gleizes, describing him as the only sports journalist imprisoned worldwide.

The journalist's lawyers have consistently maintained his innocence, arguing that he was simply carrying out his duties as a journalist. French authorities, meanwhile, have repeatedly expressed concern over his conviction and called for his release.

According to de La Saussay, Gleizes has been treated respectfully by prison staff, while his family has been able to visit him approximately once every three months, depending on authorities' sporadic approval of their visa applications.

What is Gleizes accused of?

Among the accusations levelled against Gleizes is that he travelled to Algeria as a tourist, rather than with a work permit.

"He feared, as is the case in most situations, that he wouldn't be granted one. He admitted this during his trial", Director of Advocacy and Support at media freedom NGO Reporters Sans Frontières (RSF) Antoine Bernard told Euronews.

The charges against him are also tied to his contacts with an official from the Jeunesse sportive de Kabylie (JSK) football club, based in the northeastern Kabylia region. The official in question was a member of the Movement for the Self-Determination of Kabylie (MAK), designated as a terrorist organisation by Algerian authorities in 2021.

However, according to RSF, the evidence gathered during the investigation showed that most of Gleizes' contacts with the official dated back to 2015 and 2017, before the MAK received this designation. Their only exchange in 2024 concerned preparations for his report on the club. His lawyers have argued that the investigation uncovered no material evidence of terrorist propaganda or support for the movement.

"He has been a journalist since the age of fifteen, and it is easily verifiable that he has never advocated terrorism", said Bernard, who argued that a review of Gleizes' journalistic career did not reveal any evidence of propaganda or activities directed against Algeria either.

"The key word in this case is 'emptiness.' Why, under these circumstances, has Christophe Gleizes, a journalist, been imprisoned for 500 days?", asked Bernard.

France and Algeria's diplomatic standoff

Diplomatic relations between France and Algeria soured in 2024 following Paris' recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in July, followed by the arrest of Boualem Sansal in November.

Algeria has been without an ambassador in Paris since July 2024, after it recalled its diplomatic representative. Visa restrictions have also emerged as a major source of friction between Paris and Algiers.

Relations have shown signs of improvement over the course of 2025, with a series of high-level visits aimed at restoring security, judicial and migration cooperation. Nevertheless, Gleizes' detention remains a key point of tension.

EU Ambassador to Qatar Antonino Maggiore tells Euronews that Europe plans to strengthen defence cooperation with Qatar and the Gulf countries, as "every crisis brings opportunities," while also deepening political and economic cooperation with the region.

The European Union and Qatar are deepening their defence cooperation, and "security is fundamental in the current geopolitical context and it's a mutual interest," the EU's new ambassador to Qatar Antonino Maggiore told Euronews in Doha.

Maggiore described the EU's defence cooperation thrust in Qatar and the Gulf countries as following two main objectives: connecting private defence industries through a new platform and presenting the EU's common defence industry policies to Qatar and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries.

In a wide-ranging interview with Euronews at the start of his mandate in Qatar, Maggiore said that the EU and Qatar are organising a seminar on defence technology and artificial intelligence in Doha on 3 December, to connect private-to-private industries, "to create a platform for our defence industry to work together with the Qataris counterpart and possibly also from the GCC."

Maggiore said the EU wants to build on existing defence partnerships between Qatar and individual European countries, including France, Italy, Spain and Germany.

"My personal ambition is how the European Union can add value," he said.

The seminar will also give the European Commission an opportunity to outline its plans towards the common European defence industry and discuss possible future partnerships with countries outside the bloc.

"There is a debate ongoing in the European Union on how, especially with the new multi-annual financial framework, which is our budget, how we can explore the possibility to strengthen partnership with third-party countries, also as EU, in the defence sector," Maggiore said.

The defence talks follow an EU-GCC summit scheduled for 24 October that was postponed due to ongoing tensions in the Gulf.

Maggiore acknowledged the setback but said both sides remained committed to strengthening relations.

"I think every crisis brings opportunities," Maggiore told Euronews.

"It's a missed opportunity that we have to postpone, but there is no postponement of the objectives and the urgency of strengthening the relations," he said. "There is a reciprocal wish of each other, the European Union, Qatar, the GCC."

The ambassador pointed to a recent visit to Doha by EU Special Representative for the Gulf Luigi Di Maio as evidence that diplomatic engagement was continuing unabated.

"I think where we can do more is on concrete projects of cooperation," Maggiore said.

EU backs Qatar's mediation efforts

Maggiore praised Qatar's role in mediating between the United States and Iran, saying the EU wanted to support Doha's efforts to ease regional tensions.

He highlighted a recent telephone conversation between the European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas and Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani.

The ambassador also addressed efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping restrictions have disrupted global trade, saying the EU and Qatar shared the same position on freedom of navigation through the waterway.

"No fees, no tolls for the freedom of navigation," Maggiore said, referring to the EU's position.

On Gaza, Maggiore acknowledged divisions among EU member states over the conflict.

"Member states currently have different positions on the crisis in Gaza, and of course this is a challenge for us," he said.

He added that the EU remained committed to humanitarian assistance and diplomatic efforts to end the crisis.

Maggiore also said he wanted to see closer economic ties, particularly in transport.

He confirmed that European Commissioner for Transport Apostolos Tzitzikostas would visit Doha for the upcoming Doha Forum in December to discuss connectivity with Qatar and other Gulf partners.

"Connectivity is a pillar, I think, where we can foster and boost our economic ties," he said.

The EU is also working on an initiative called Connect EU, aimed at bringing European businesses together with Qatari companies.

Maggiore identified two priorities he hopes to advance over the next year: visa liberalisation for Qatari citizens and negotiations on a strategic partnership agreement.

He said making travel easier would help strengthen ties between people in Europe and Qatar.

The proposed strategic partnership agreement would provide a broader framework for cooperation, something Maggiore hopes to see progress on within the next year.

"We do need a framework," he said, stressing the political will on both sides to strengthen the partnership.

Over the past year, Europe has tried to attract researchers who no longer feel comfortable working in the United States’ academic system under the Donald Trump administration due to budget cuts and policy shifts. But did it succeed?

On 1 October, the European Commission announced an extra €210 million to the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA), the European Union (EU) flagship grant scheme supporting doctoral education and postdoctoral training.

Since its establishment in 1996, the programme has supported more than 150,000 researchers and this additional funding is set to finance over 700 more across 2026 and 2027.

Although relevant, this boost is expected to have a limited impact due to the record-breaking number of MSCA applications in the latest years. For instance, the 2026 MSCA postdoctoral fellowship call alone received more than 21,500 applications.

The measure announced by the Commission is part of Choose Europe, a broader EU initiative launched in May 2025 to attract academics and innovators to Europe.

Back then, some researchers had started considering leaving the United States (US) in response to budget cuts and policy shifts under the Donald Trump administration, an opportunity Europe tried to seize by positioning itself as an alternative.

But did the EU do enough to become a leading destination for researchers?

After spending countless hours speaking with academics to unpack complex scientific topics, Euronews Tech Talks dives into the state of European academia through the voices of leading professors and young researchers from across the continent.

Is Europe doing enough to attract academics from the US?

Since the start of Donald Trump’s second presidential mandate, research in the US has faced several challenges. Budget cuts, visa-related problems and crackdowns on campus protests have fuelled the debate on whether the country is still a good place for scientists.

In response, Europe has tried to attract talent from the US, launching both regional and national plans.

However, according to Helga Nowotny, former president of the European Research Council, these strategies have some flaws. “The intention was a good one, but the way Europe went about it was, and I'm sorry to say that, not well coordinated,” she said.

Nowotny noted that the strategy was too fragmented, with member states, universities and EU institutions almost competing among themselves.

“We are now in a more realistic phase, and we should concentrate on getting young people because the situation for young researchers in the US is getting very difficult,” she added.

With the rise of more extremist political groups around Europe, however, Nowotny thinks the EU should not take its academic freedom and scientific values for granted.

“We have to be very attentive and not fall into the trap of the illusion that just because some countries have written in their constitution the freedom of science, that this is all that is needed,” she said.

Is Europe doing enough to keep academics?

Attracting researchers to Europe, however, is only the first step.

According to Orla Feely, president of University College Dublin, Ireland, there are technical factors that Europe needs to work on to keep researchers on the continent: visa permits, strong pathways to industry and building an environment where people not only want to work, but also to live.

Particularly, Europe seems to struggle to translate research into innovation. “We know that we have great research in Europe, but we also know that as you advance further along the competitiveness spectrum, that Europe has fallen behind other countries,” Feely said.

Yet Feely is positive that things will improve: “There are a lot of things that we need to get right, but I think people are increasingly aware of these and are working together so that we join up the undoubted talent coming out of European universities and turn it into competitive advantage”.

According to Manuel Heitor, professor and former Portugal minister of science, technology and higher education, the problem in Europe is not the innovation gap.

“What we are facing is an investment gap that actually then results in an innovation gap,” he told Euronews Next. “We need to recognise that we need to align and accelerate research and innovation, and this will require an adequate funding level and better governance,” he added.

This is a crucial time to talk about investment and allocation of EU resources. Discussions are ongoing in the EU on the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the long-term budget plan for 2028-2034.

Based on the proposal presented by the Irish Presidency of the European Council on 10 October, the budget of Horizon Europe, the EU’s key funding programme for research and innovation, would be €158 billion, an amount that certain universities have criticised as a reduction compared to the European Commission proposal.
