Christine Lagarde's early departure will not delay the digital euro, a European Central Bank official stated at the Web Summit in Lisbon, citing the pilot due next year and a pledge by Brussels to agree the law by the end of 2026, while dismissing fears the project threatens people's privacy.

Christine Lagarde's early exit as president of the European Central Bank will not hold up the digital euro, an ECB official said on Tuesday at the Web Summit in Lisbon, one of Europe's largest technology conferences.

Alessandro Giovannini, adviser to the programme manager of the digital euro project, pointed to the pilot starting next year and a commitment by EU lawmakers to agree the law by the end of the year.

"I'm not afraid that any change or anything will impact it, because this is a strategic project," Giovannini stated at a panel moderated by Euronews, calling the digital euro "a European project" rather than the ECB's alone.

Lagarde announced last month that she would step down on 7 February 2027, almost nine months early.

Germany's Isabel Schnabel also departs the six-member Executive Board, the ECB's top management team, in January, and chief economist Philip Lane's mandate expires in May.

As Euronews previously reported, Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot are currently the two main candidates to succeed Lagarde.

Final stretch in Brussels

In March, EU leaders called for negotiations on the digital euro law to be concluded by the end of this year, ahead of the pilot programme scheduled for 2027.

"This is the commitment that we have from the co-legislators," Giovannini said, meaning the European Parliament and EU governments.

The two sides have been in trilogues, three-way negotiations with the European Commission that form the last stage of EU law-making, since July. The latest round was last Thursday, and Ireland, which chairs the talks for member states, is reportedly aiming for a deal on 18 November.

How the fees merchants pay are calculated, part of the digital euro's business model, is one of the issues still unresolved.

This is significant, as the ECB aims to be ready for a first issuance in 2029, while technical preparations are progressing independently of the ongoing discussions in Brussels.

In July, the ECB picked 36 banks and payment firms, including Deutsche Bank, UniCredit and Stripe, for a 12-month pilot starting in the second half of 2027. Last month, it chose network providers, including payments firm Nexi and telecoms group Telefónica, to connect them to its platform.

The first pilot transactions will come "in less than one year", Giovannini said, adding that the firms building the system were all "European companies controlled by other European companies".

Banks will not pay for the shared infrastructure, as Giovannini explained it would be "paid by the ECB" and "offered for free by the ECB to everyone".

The ECB has estimated development will cost around €1.3 billion before a first issuance, and running the system about €320 million a year from 2029, costs that eurozone central banks would bear, as with banknotes.

Is Europe behind?

Europe trails China, which has been piloting its digital yuan since 2019, and the US has taken the opposite path with the GENIUS Act, passed last year, which left the field to private stablecoins, crypto tokens pegged to a currency such as the US dollar.

"The best moment to plant a tree was yesterday," Giovannini acknowledged, adding that "Europe has its own time and we need to also accept the legislative pace that comes with that."

Ultimately what mattered, he said, was "that we are not losing time".

The wait until 2029 reflects the scale of the task, Giovannini noted, with more than 4,000 payment providers and millions of merchants to coordinate with.

The digital euro aims to cut Europe's reliance on international card schemes such as Visa and Mastercard. ECB board member Piero Cipollone said last week that in 13 eurozone countries, card payments in shops run entirely through non-European firms.

Unlike China, which since January has let banks pay interest on digital yuan wallets, the digital euro will pay no interest.

"As you don't get yields on your banknote, you're not going to get yields on the digital euro," Giovannini said, though banks and fintech firms could offer their own rewards.

Privacy fears

Critics warn a central bank digital currency could let the state monitor, or even control, people's spending, but Giovannini disagreed.

Handing a €20 banknote across the stage, he said offline digital euros, sent by tapping phones without an internet connection, would work like cash.

"I'm tapping your phone and no one will know that I've given €20 to you," he explained.

The system would only check that the token was genuine, leaving "no digital footprint that this comes from me and went to you, or comes from my bank".

However, such payments will be subject to limits, which lawmakers have been negotiating, to curb money laundering and terrorist financing risks.

For online payments, banks would know who paid whom, as they do today, but the ECB would only see pseudonymised data.

"The ECB that is in between will never see anything," Giovannini guaranteed, contrasting this with the card schemes that sit in the middle of payment rails today.

More than half of all female Bundeswehr soldiers have already experienced sexual misconduct, a hidden-figure study shows, revealing up to five times more cases than officially reported.

More than 60% of women serving in Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, have experienced sexual misconduct ranging from lewd remarks to physical harassment, according to a new study presented by Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, of the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD), on Wednesday.

The study set out to measure the true extent of unreported cases. In an anonymous online survey, respondents were able to answer 41 detailed questions. The results paint a shocking picture.

“The extent of sexualised misconduct far exceeds the known reporting figures,” Pistorius said in a statement after presenting the report. Fewer than a third of cases were reported.

“The study shows that the extent of sexualised misconduct is 3 to 5 times higher than the reported cases,” added Inspector General Carsten Breuer, Germany’s most senior military officer.

The results confirm that sexual violence and harassment are a systemic problem within the Bundeswehr. Industry representatives fear the report could deter women from applying to join.

“Respect for human dignity is our highest constitutional principle. Alongside mutual respect, collegiality, comradeship and responsible leadership, it is one of the core values of our Bundeswehr,” Pistorius writes in a foreword to the armed forces’ action plan against sexualised misconduct.

“Sexualised violence and sexualised misconduct are incompatible with this value base and have no place in the Bundeswehr,” he continued. The defence minister expects all members of the armed forces to treat one another with respect.

Four levels of sexual violence in the Bundeswehr

Of the soldiers who answered the questionnaire, 4,000 said they had been subjected to sexual harassment during their service. Extrapolated, this corresponds to more than 60% of soldiers.

“Those particularly often affected, which is no surprise either, are young women in the lower rank groups,” Pistorius said in a statement. Among men, non-heterosexual soldiers are disproportionately affected. “Perpetrators are overwhelmingly men,” the defence minister said.

The survey used a four-level system. In the first category, respondents could indicate whether they had been subjected to sexualised remarks or lewd comments. Almost 40% of servicewomen and 16% of servicemen surveyed reported such experiences.

Fifteen percent said they had been harassed with images taken against their will or altered using artificial intelligence. Nine percent of servicewomen and 3% of servicemen said they had been physically assaulted, while 2% of both women and men said they had experienced outright sexual violence in the Bundeswehr.

It remains unclear whether the real figures are even higher than those found by the study. Around a third of servicewomen and servicemen also said they had not reported sexual misconduct because they did not trust their superiors or doubted they would carry out a serious investigation.

Pistorius presents action plan

Pistorius has made clear on several occasions that he has a zero-tolerance approach to sexual misconduct. His words are now to be followed by an action plan.

According to the Bundeswehr, the plan rests on three pillars. The first is prevention. “Dealing with sexualised misconduct will become a mandatory part of qualification programmes in the Bundeswehr,” the armed forces said of the action plan.

“Sexualised misconduct will become a topic in training at all levels from the very beginning,” Breuer said in a statement when presenting the study’s findings.

The second pillar is making investigations more professional, with clear points of contact, reporting lines and procedures.

Disciplinary punishments are also to be announced publicly to a soldier’s unit, a sanction known as “announcement before the troops”. This transparency is intended to strengthen the confidence of those affected and to act as a deterrent within the ranks.

Pistorius said there was not only a lack of knowledge about reporting channels, but also a lack of trust in them. For him, this also means tackling misconduct consistently. “Anyone who is not a role model, even tolerates misconduct or does not deal with it consistently, will no longer hold a leadership position.”

Finally, the action plan addresses support for those affected. Among the options being discussed is an anonymous reporting point, so that people considering whether to come forward no longer have to rely on trusting a superior. At the end of October, Breuer set up a hotline at short notice.

Under the name “HELP”, victims of sexual harassment can report incidents and receive counselling. According to Pistorius, the letters stand for the German words for support, initial counselling, guidance and prevention support.

The service currently runs from 8am to 6pm, but it is to be available 24 hours a day in future. Those affected are also to receive psychosocial support during investigations.

Pistorius set out his aim: “Every person in our Bundeswehr must be able to rely on respect, protection and fair treatment.”

Breuer added: “Only those who have this security and this trust can be ready for deployment.”

Politicians call for changes

Politicians, particularly from the Greens, have repeatedly called for an external body.

There must be an “external reporting office” outside the units, so that servicewomen would not have to report such incidents only to their superiors, said Sara Nanni, security policy spokesperson for the Greens. She was speaking to public broadcaster ZDF’s Morgenmagazin programme before the figures were published.

“I believe that very few women can get through a week without hearing a remark that is also a form of sexualised verbal violence,” said Nanni, who sits on the defence committee of the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament.

Thomas Erndl, defence policy spokesperson for the conservative CDU/CSU parliamentary group, known as the Union, said on Tuesday: “Anyone who humiliates female or male comrades, violates their dignity or denies women the right to serve as equals in the Bundeswehr fundamentally violates soldiers’ self-image and the values of Innere Führung.”

Innere Führung is the Bundeswehr’s guiding principle that soldiers are “citizens in uniform” bound by democratic values. Erndl welcomed the planned intervention office, which is to be reachable around the clock.

The study was commissioned by Eva Högl, the former Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces, shortly before the end of her term in 2024. The commissioner acts as the German parliament’s military ombudsperson. The survey was carried out by the Bundeswehr Centre of Military History and Social Sciences in Potsdam.

The researchers contacted around 25,000 servicewomen and servicemen, about 18% of whom responded. They consider the results to be a representative picture of the armed forces. Some respondents were no longer serving at the time.

According to Pistorius, the study is to be repeated at regular intervals.

A large-scale prisoner exchange emerged as the only tangible result of two days of US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, with no breakthrough on a ceasefire or territorial disputes.

Ukraine and Russia have agreed in principle to a major prisoner exchange following two days of US-mediated peace talks in Abu Dhabi, although negotiations ended without a breakthrough on the central issues dividing the two sides, Euronews reports from the UAE.

US envoy Jared Kushner announced the agreement on Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, saying the final number of prisoners to be exchanged would be determined on Thursday.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalise the numbers tomorrow," Kushner said.

Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Medinsky also confirmed the planned exchange, although neither side provided further details on its timing or scale.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that negotiators had been discussing an exchange of 1,000 prisoners from each side, potentially rising to 1,500 each.

The agreement marks the most concrete — and so far the only — outcome of the first direct negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow in nine months, following an earlier round in Geneva in February this year that failed to produce a breakthrough.

During negotiations in Istanbul in May 2025, the two countries also agreed to exchange 1,000 prisoners each despite failing to reach a ceasefire agreement.

US envoys head to Moscow

Kushner said he and Steve Witkoff would travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, before heading to Dublin for talks with Zelenskyy.

Russia continues to insist that Ukraine withdraw from territory in the eastern Donbas region still under Kyiv's control, while Zelenskyy has maintained that territorial decisions must be addressed at the leaders' level.

Moscow has also rejected calls for an immediate ceasefire, insisting on broader security arrangements before agreeing to halt hostilities.

European representatives were present in Abu Dhabi for separate consultations with Ukrainian and US officials but did not participate directly in the trilateral negotiations.

Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said his delegation had not held talks with European representatives and questioned their presence.

"No, we did not communicate with them. We don't really understand in what capacity they are here," Medinsky told reporters.

He also said Moscow received no concrete peace initiatives or proposals from European countries, questioning what there was to discuss with them.

"We don't really understand what there is to discuss with them," he told reporters.

Umerov said Kyiv's delegation would hold further discussions with European partners on Wednesday.

Washington indicated that European countries should eventually join the negotiations, particularly as discussions expand to the continent's future security arrangements.

The popular Aegean island, having first regulated cruise tourism, is now implementing a plan to increase winter arrivals by promoting activities beyond the famous sunset over the Caldera.

Santorini is considered the most popular Greek island worldwide. Its distinctive volcanic caldera, whitewashed houses and sunsets in Oia consistently place it among the top choices for international travellers. However, over the past two years local hoteliers have been complaining that their hotels are not filling up with tourists.

"After the Covid pandemic we had intense tourist activity on our island, but because of some unrelated events, one was the seismic activity on the neighbouring islands and later on the war in the Gulf, we experienced a drop in tourism," hotel owner Thomas Giannis tells Euronews. "For me personally it was around 30 to 40%."

The biggest decline was recorded in arrivals of tourists from the United States and, of course, from Israel. The former in particular, who tend to spend a lot of money in the destinations they visit and are therefore especially sought after by people working in tourism, book their holiday packages up until early spring, in other words during the periods that coincided with the seismic activity events of 2025 and the start of the war with Iran this year.

Greece may have been far from the centre of operations, but this is not immediately obvious to the average American planning a holiday.

Despite the downturn, the situation improved after the summer, according to Thira Mayor Nikos Zorzos. "Tourism in Santorini started this year with a sense of numbness, but the situation then stabilised. September and October are strong tourist months and attract visitors who have a special interest in the island," the mayor tells Euronews.

Gastronomy and culture

What do we mean by "special interests"? Thomas Giannis explains: "Santorini is not just a summer destination to watch a sunset. It is also a gastronomic and cultural destination. And it can now offer tourism all year round."

With this in mind, it was recently announced that a new digital campaign of 32 short videos will be launched, aiming to broaden the island’s international tourism image by showcasing experiences that are often overshadowed by its famous sunsets and luxury accommodation. These include its distinctive wine tradition, closely linked to the volcanic soil and climate of the island, its gastronomy, and visits of cultural and religious interest.

In fact, this is now what most visitors are looking for, both from the US and from the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Austria, the Netherlands, Poland, Belgium and Romania, the European countries from which most visitors come. They are joined by tourists from Australia and Asian countries such as China, South Korea and Japan, from which group trips are often organised.

In Santorini, July in particular had a strong Italian "flavour". Traffic to and from Italy reached 93,315 passengers, placing the country first among foreign markets. It was followed by the UK with 59,362 passengers and France with 35,158, while Germany recorded 17,746 passengers. Traffic with Spain was also significant at 14,443 passengers, followed by Austria with 11,211 and Romania with 10,594.

Furthermore, Thomas Giannis argues that Santorini is no longer the very expensive destination people imagine if they have never visited. "Santorini is for every budget. It can cater for everything. It has rooms from very cheap to extremely expensive," he says, disagreeing with the widespread perception that it is an off-limits destination for those on lower incomes, and stressing that especially outside the peak season there are many excellent deals.

As he also revealed, there has been a drop in tourist arrivals over the past two years, even if this is due to unrelated factors. However, this comparatively lower occupancy than in previous periods is also attributed to another factor, the constant construction of new hotel units.

"The increase in the number of beds creates an issue with accommodation occupancy," the mayor comments, adding that he has used Euronews to call on the government to take measures to stop unregulated building on the island.

Cruise tourism: 'A blessing and a curse'

On visitor numbers, Nikos Zorzos adds: "The figures are roughly the same. Santorini receives 3.5 million visitors a year including those who arrive by cruise ship."

However, locals have raised a counter-argument with the Ministry of Tourism. Because of the airport and direct flights to it from European destinations, a significant number of those recorded as landing and taking off for Santorini in fact do not stay on the island but on neighbouring ones, simply using it as a gateway into and out of the country, which in turn distorts the real figures.

Even so, there is no doubt that Santorini has plenty of tourists every year and, for cruise ships in particular, a stop there is considered a must. However, for islands like Santorini, cruise tourism is seen by many as both a blessing and a curse.

On the one hand it pushes up visitor numbers, but on the other it does not bring money to the local population and is the main reason behind the severe overcrowding that is often seen in the narrow alleyways and at times becomes unbearable.

What has the municipal authority done about this? "Look, we regulated cruise tourism," Nikos Zorzos tells Euronews. "About 10 years ago, with a study we carried out with the University of the Aegean, we set the maximum number of visitors who can visit Santorini every day. As a result there are no longer crowds in different parts of the island and movement is easier. So cruise tourism is no longer the problem it was in the past."

Now, up to 8,000 tourists a day can disembark from cruise ships. Even so, it is estimated that around half of all tourists in Santorini each year come from the cruise sector. Local residents complain that this type of visitor does not spend money on the island, since they do not stay overnight and, for the most part, do not even visit local shops. In recent years a further trend has emerged, with some not even going ashore and instead enjoying the famous caldera sunset from the ship.

"Of course, those who stay in hotels or other accommodation spend more money than visitors on short cruise stopovers," admits the mayor of Thira.

According to a ministerial decision, however, a new increased "cruise levy" has been in place since last year, essentially a per capita tax on each disembarkation. It amounts to 20 euros per person in the summer period (1 June to 30 September), drops to 12 euros in April, May and October, and is reduced to 4 euros in the winter period (1 November to 31 March). However, only one third of this money reaches the municipal coffers, as the remainder is shared between the Ministries of Tourism and Shipping.

The Cloud and AI Development Act should give Europe greater control over essential technologies while helping its own tech industry grow and compete globally, say MEPs.

A joint draft report on the European Commission's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) was presented at the European Parliament on Wednesday, calling for common EU rules on cloud and AI infrastructure, greater support for European technology companies and reduced dependence on foreign providers.

The proposal aims to strengthen Europe's digital infrastructure and international competitiveness amid concerns that reliance on foreign technology providers could undermine the bloc's control over critical services.

"This is not only a matter of economic competitiveness, it is also a matter of our capacity to make our own decisions," Spanish conservative MEP Diego Solier said during a press conference on Wednesday.

"Technological sovereignty does not consist in closing Europe to the rest of the world, it consists of ensuring that Europe has the capacity to act, compete and choose."

The proposal comes as the EU is making significant efforts to reduce its reliance on other countries for critical services, infrastructure, materials and security, with a slew of proposals currently in the works.

European leaders have been worried since Donald Trump returned to office, making the US an unreliable partner and exposing how reliant the bloc is American goods and services, especially big tech.

In June this year, Trump ordered Anthropic to block access to its widely used Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 AI models from outside the US, citing security concerns.

Access was restored later that month but conversations over so-called "kill switches" that the US government and tech companies held over critical European civilian and military infrastructure only intensified.

Boosting Europe's digital independence

The draft report calls for greater investment in European cloud and AI infrastructure, including measures to help European technology companies grow.

It also seeks to establish common EU standards for cloud services and strengthen protections for critical sectors, including healthcare, energy and transport.

"Our critical systems run on someone else's technology, and someone else can switch it off. Today a court, tomorrow a ministry, a hospital, a grid operator?," Dutch green MEP Reinier Van Lanschot warned.

The lawmakers also want public authorities to buy more cloud services from European providers to help them compete with foreign companies.

"Europe has brilliant businesses and they are not asking for subsidies, they are asking for customers. That's at the heart of our proposal," Van Lanschot said.

The report also calls for faster approval procedures for new data centres, while ensuring that projects respect environmental requirements and benefit local communities.

Under the Commission's proposal, the EU aims to triple its data centre capacity over the next five to seven years.

The proposed legislation comes amid concerns over Europe's dependence on non-EU technology companies.

According to the Commission, three non-European hyperscale cloud providers control more than 70% of the European cloud market, raising concerns about data sovereignty, security and operational autonomy.

What happens next?

The draft report is expected to be published on Thursday and discussed by European parliamentary committees on 1 December.

A committee vote is provisionally scheduled for mid-March 2027, followed by a plenary vote in April next year.

"It’s no longer science fiction or just a single demo aircraft," Michael Du, vice president and chief financial officer of Chinese company XPeng, told Euronews Next.

People could start travelling in so-called flying cars in China as soon as summer 2027, the manufacturer of a two-seater autopilot vehicle told Euronews Next.

The low-altitude flying device by XPeng Aridge is close to large-scale commercialisation, with limited deliveries to partners in China expected within months and a wider roll-out to follow, and has been approved by China’s civil aviation authorities for limited use.

"It’s no longer science fiction or just a single demo aircraft," vice president and chief financial officer of Chinese company XPeng Michael Du said at the Web Summit technology event in Lisbon. "It’s really a commercial model."

The two-seat electric vehicle costs $300,000 (€270,000) and has a cockpit the size of a small car.

The company has received more than 7,000 pre-orders worldwide, "most of them in China, but also some from the Middle East," Du said.

Buyers include individuals interested in personal flying and air tourism, as well as operators in emergency rescue and public services. "It showcases how wide a range of applications our products are capable of," he said.

The aircraft has completed its technical test flights across a range of conditions. "We tried it at sea level, high altitude, cold areas, hot areas, extreme wind or even rainy areas, a lot of extreme cases, so it’s safe," Du said.

The company has spent a decade building the technology from its own mass-production factory in Guangzhou.

The aircraft has completed its technical test flights, including at sea level and high altitude and in cold, hot, windy and rainy conditions.

It has also received a type inspection authorisation from the Civil Aviation Administration of China, whose test pilots completed all the test items. The company is now going through final type certification.

The future of mobility

Electric aircraft will reshape transport the way electrification reshaped cars, according to Du.

"Electrification has transformed and advanced the development of the car industry. Similar patterns will happen in the aircraft industry," he said, citing better power distribution, more redundancies and quieter operation.

Asked how the aircraft could change mobility in the long term, the executive used a Chinese saying about roads.

"In China, there’s a saying: if you want to develop the economy, you’d better build the roads," the executive said. "When you have better roads, it’s more accessible to everyone else."

That logic held while most travel happened on the ground, he said, but air mobility offers "a different format to improve transportation efficiency".

It "will completely change how people travel over time, from an efficiency perspective, from an economics perspective," he said.

The main advantage, the executive said, is that aircraft skip the need for continuous infrastructure. "You don’t actually need to build infrastructure inch by inch from the starting point to the end," he said. "That’s the case for cars. That’s the case for high-speed rail."

The device could also benefit island nations and sparsely populated regions, Du said, "those areas will become so valuable" once air mobility arrives, as it will create economic value.

When will it come to Europe?

After China, the company plans to work with overseas regulators and partners, with the Middle East and Southeast Asia as the clearest early markets.

But Europe is "definitely a very attractive market", Du said, adding that the company hopes Web Summit will introduce European consumers, regulators and partners to the product.

However, Du said there were hurdles to overcome before entering Europe, including launching an affordable product at launch, and having the right infrastructure and places to fly to.

Geopolitics

Asked about US-China tensions, Du said the company would welcome more open markets and would be happy to enter the United States if regulations allow.

He noted that China, the US and Europe together account for only about half of the global aircraft market, so a temporary lack of access to one still leaves plenty of room to grow.

Du compared the situation to Chinese electric cars, which have now become widely accepted in Europe.

"Starting small, starting from outside the city, starting with some cargo, some passenger carrying, gradually into larger ones, entering into cities," Du said. "I think that could be one way the industry develops more positively."

SRI, prin Centrul Național Cyberint, a identificat atacul în decembrie 2025 și a implementat măsuri de contracarare și de remediere a efectelor.

Specialiștii explică faptul că “atacatorii au exploatat o serie de vulnerabilități sistemice la nivelul sistemelor de operare Microsoft, însă în urma intervenției Centrului Național Cyberint atacul a fost oprit. De asemenea, SRI a informat beneficiarii legali și, totodată, aspectele respective au făcut obiectul cooperării cu partenerii europeni, la nivelul comunității de intelligence, precum și cu cei de la nivelul UE și NATO”.

SRI precizează că are în derulare măsuri investigative complexe care vizează și alte secvențe conexate cu campanii cibernetice implementate de Federația Rusă.

Incidentul a fost semnalat, marți, de specialiștii companiei de securitate cibernetică ESET. Instituția în cauză nu a fost numită nici de SRI, nici de ESET. Compania a detaliat că atacul a avut loc prin intermediul serviciului Microsoft Exchange. 

ESET a explicat că pe 28 noiembrie anul trecut, a descoperit setul de instrumente care instalează un cod care examinează e-mail-uri pe un server Exchange al unei organizații guvernamentale din Kazahstan: “Ceea ce inițial părea a fi o serie de componente suspecte separate s-a dovedit curând a fi un set de instrumente nedocumentat până atunci – o colecție de malware modular .NET concepută pentru a rula pe servere Microsoft Exchange, a primi comenzi, a le executa în memorie, a cartografia organizația compromisă și a colecta mesaje de e-mail selectate. După ce ne-am perfecționat metodele de detectare, am descoperit același set de instrumente la o organizație guvernamentală din România – compromisă pe 23 decembrie 2025 – unde era configurat să identifice e-mailurile trimise către sau primite de la Organizația Tratatului Atlanticului de Nord (NATO) și de la Uniunea Europeană (UE)”.

Specialiștii ESET arată că Turla, cunoscută și ca Snake, este activă cel puțin din 2004 și, în general, este considerată ca făcând parte din Serviciul Federal de Securitate al Federației Ruse (FSB). Țintele sale obișnuite sunt guvernele, misiunile diplomatice și organizațiile din domeniul apărării, în principal din Europa, Asia Centrală și Orientul Mijlociu.

Cave continued, regarding AI’s increasing role in new music: “Song generator platforms are, in my view, indicators of this nascent technology’s demonic potential to hollow out human endeavour and sever our connection to the divine."

"They mock creation itself by rendering humanity unnecessary, taking the fruits of human striving and reducing them to mere products. It is, perhaps, our final, most soul-destroying humiliation,” he explained.

The musician has been a vocal critic of artificial intelligence, calling it “unbelievably disturbing” in the past and previously telling ChatGPT to "fuck off and leave songwriting alone". He also revealed that he received numerous submissions of AI-generated song lyrics written "in the style of Nick Cave", which he called "a grotesque mockery of what it is to be human”.

He did appear to soften his stance last year. Replying to a fan-submitted question asking if changing an opinion is a sign of weakness, relating to director Andrew Donminik's 'Tupelo' film (which uses AI), Cave admitted that changing one’s once-rigid opinions could be a sign of strength.

“As I watched Andrew’s surreal little film, I felt my view of AI as an artistic device soften. To some extent, my mind was changed,” Cave wrote about the AI-powered video made to mark the 40th anniversary of his song 'Tupelo'. He admitted that the footage was “uncanny”, as the video used AI to animate still archival images of Elvis Presley.

At the time, Cave said that the AI-animated photographs of Presley “had an uncanny quality, as if he had been raised from the dead, and the crucifixion-resurrection images at the end were both shocking and deeply affecting.”

Now, it seems that Cave is back to condemning generative AI in all its forms - specifically when used for songwriting.

When asked by another fan whether art can be separated by the artist - a debate that has followed artists and culture fans for centuries - Cave replied: “We cannot separate the art from the artists, for they are as inseparable as the waves from the sea they rise from. That may be an uncomfortable truth for some but, for me, the matter was settled. Until now."

He continued: “With the advent of song generation platforms, the thorny issue has been upended. At last, the artist can be separated from the art. Not just that, the artist – that flawed, messy, broken, woeful, joyful problem – can be removed from the equation altogether, like so much dross.”

Taking aim at the AI song generator Suno, he went on: “Suno, the Great Cancellator, which has never loved or laughed or grieved, never experienced joy or loss or heartbreak, never felt boredom or its adjacent epiphany, produces an imitation of the soul – a song – in fifteen seconds flat. This is an affront to any songwriter who has lived and struggled in this world and earned the right to create a song.”

He concluded: “For those eager to rid the world of problematic artists – for these censorious forces remain persistent – it is surely cause for celebration, as these platforms promise to rid the world of artists altogether.”

The most recent Nick Cave And The Bad Seeds album is 2024's 'Wild God' - which made Euronews Culture's Best Albums of 2024 end of year list.

Cave recently announced a North American tour for 2027 that will see him answer questions from fans and perform stripped-back versions of his songs on the piano. Tickets for the new 'Conversations With Nick Cave: An Evening Of Talk And Music' tour go on sale on Friday (13 November).

The paper said security services and censors forced it to stop operating after they evicted it, shut down its donation system, blocked its printing, and revoked its media registration.

Novaya Gazeta, Russia's last remaining newspaper openly critical of the Kremlin and Moscow's ongoing all-out war in Ukraine, has closed after authorities stripped it of its media registration and severed its ability to operate, the newspaper said.

In a statement on 30 October, the paper said security services and censors had "forced the editorial team to cease its activities."

The newsroom was ordered to vacate its premises, its reader donation system was shut down, its online resources were blocked, its printing arrangements were terminated, and state censors at printing facilities refused to allow the paper to publish, before its media registration was revoked.

"Elections and elected bodies of power have in effect been abolished, civil society institutions destroyed, freedom of conscience and human dignity trampled underfoot," the newspaper said in its farewell statement.

Editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov held a final editorial meeting attended by staff, founder and Nobel laureate Dmitry Muratov and journalists from other outlets.

Staff packed their belongings and took down from the walls the portraits of murdered colleagues, among them Anna Politkovskaya, Yuri Shchekochikhin and Natalya Estemirova.

Muratov described repression in Russia as "overwhelming," saying that by 2021, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of people had already been convicted under relevant statutes.

"This is because the country is not run by parliament, or by local administrations or governors, but by the FSB of the Russian Federation," he said.

In his farewell address to staff, Muratov made several requests: to support Russians opposed to the war, to push for the release of political prisoners, to seek a humanitarian corridor for villages in the former area of Oleshky, and to work to stop Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities.

"The light, heat and water in cities in Ukraine could be wiped off the face of the Earth. These cities will be poured into sacks like dust. This madness, this slaughter must be stopped," he said.

Muratov also said more than 400,000 of the newspaper's articles had been archived and were being republished worldwide.

"We will go on living, and I am sure that this country, which is going through such hard times, will sooner or later come to its senses. As soon as the first signs of this appear, Novaya Gazeta will return to our readers and colleagues," Sokolov said in his address to those gathered outside the building.

Reporters Without Borders, Amnesty International and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned Russia's closure of the newspaper.

The Kremlin dismissed its significance, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov stating that "some media outlets cease to exist and new ones take their place," which he called a "normal process".

Novaya Gazeta was founded in 1993 and became known for its coverage of the Chechen wars and its investigations into human rights abuses and corruption.

Six of its journalists were murdered. Russian authorities had designated it a "foreign agent", but the paper continued to publish until its final closure.

After the journalists left, a new sign appeared on the wall alongside the newspaper's nameplate: "Novaya Gazeta lived here."

Four drones and dozens of suspected meteorological balloon sightings were detected moving from Belarus towards NATO's external border.

NATO fighter jets twice tried and failed to shoot down a drone over northern Lithuania overnight, as unidentified aerial objects triggered air-raid warnings across the Baltic states and prompted precautionary restrictions in Finland.

Three unmanned aircraft were initially detected operating in Belarusian airspace and moving north towards Latvia. Latvia’s armed forces subsequently reported that two additional aerial targets entered Latvian airspace from the direction of Belarus and later departed.

A fourth drone crossed from Belarus into Lithuania at around 1.20am local time (12.20am CET). It briefly entered Polish airspace before abruptly changing direction and returning to Lithuania.

NATO fighter jets tracked it as it travelled north towards the Latvian border, but two attempts to destroy it near Biržai, in northern Lithuania, were unsuccessful. One of the missiles fired by the fighter jets missed the drone and fell to the ground.

The drone subsequently crossed into Latvia, where fighters on NATO’s air policing mission could not get into position to shoot it down, allowing it to cross into Estonia and eventually into Russia.

The drone’s type, origin and whether it was carrying explosives remain unknown.

“We do not currently have confirmed information about the type of drone,” Rear Admiral Giedrius Premeneckas, chief of the Lithuanian Armed Forces Defence Staff, said at a press briefing early on Wednesday. It was not yet possible to determine whether the aircraft was Ukrainian or Russian, he added.

Ukraine had carried out a large-scale drone attack on Russia overnight and, according to Premeneckas, one possibility was that the aircraft had been diverted from its intended course by electronic warfare measures. But he stressed that this remained an assumption.

Overnight, authorities in all three Baltic states issued warnings urging residents to seek shelter as unidentified aerial objects approached or entered their airspace. Further north, Finland temporarily restricted aviation and maritime activity in the eastern Gulf of Finland, close to the Russian border.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda called the night “restless and difficult” in a Facebook post, warning that more incursions were possible.

“Unfortunately, as long as Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine continues, the incursion of combat drones into Lithuanian territory may happen again,” Nausėda said, calling on Lithuanians to “remain patient and understanding.”

The latest incident follows a series of drone incursions across the Baltic region in recent months.

In October, a suspected drone entered Lithuanian airspace and exploded in the country’s north, triggering air-raid alerts and prompting NATO fighter jets to scramble. In September, NATO aircraft also shot down a drone over Lithuania, while an earlier incident in May saw a Romanian NATO fighter jet destroy a suspected Ukrainian drone over Estonia after it entered from Russia. Latvia has also reported repeated incursions, including a drone that struck an oil storage facility in May.

Wave of suspected meteorological balloons

In Lithuania, the drone activity on Tuesday night coincided with a separate wave of suspected meteorological balloons, further complicating the overnight response.

Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre, described the night as “the most unsettled in the country’s history,” citing both the drone incidents and the balloons.

He also noted that Belarusian authorities had informed Lithuania about objects detected on their side of the border that could potentially be moving towards Lithuanian airspace.

“This is a welcome development. Such cases have been rare recently,” he said, referring to the information passed on by Belarus.

Around 10 balloon-related radar sightings were recorded, disrupting airport operations. Aircraft were allowed to depart, but landing operations were restricted, affecting three flights and forcing around 470 passengers to change their plans, Vitkauskas said.

He also warned against disinformation circulating online suggesting Lithuania was allowing Ukrainian drones to use its airspace to attack Russia.

“That is an absolute lie,” he said, urging residents to follow official emergency instructions and not to ignore alerts sent to their phones.

The National Security Commission was also due to discuss access to public shelters on Wednesday, with Vitkauskas acknowledging that reaching shelters during a night-time emergency can be difficult. Residents without access to a shelter were advised to follow the two-wall principle, stay away from windows and seek refuge in a basement where possible.

“The events of last night will be thoroughly investigated,” Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said in a Facebook post.

Luxury brand Four Seasons is taking travel to another level with a 23-day private jet journey around the world.

Launching in May 2028, the new itinerary will whisk guests from San Francisco to Seoul, Sri Lanka, Zanzibar and the French Riviera, with exclusive cultural experiences, yacht trips and stays at some of the hotel group's most prestigious properties along the way.

The original Four Seasons Private Jet launched in 2015, and the current, custom-built Airbus A321LR aircraft has been in service since early 2021.

The “coastlines and culture” itinerary will take flight from 6–26 May for just 48 guests but, unsurprisingly for such a high-end brand, it won’t come cheap. Tickets start from a staggering €213,000 per person.

If you can afford it, though, it’s set to be a pretty magical experience.

"With ‘coastlines and culture’, we're able to bring together destinations rarely experienced within a single journey, creating moments of awe and discovery, and opening the door to experiences guests may never have imagined possible, all grounded in the genuine care and thoughtful service that define Four Seasons,” said Marc Speichert, executive vice president and chief commercial officer at Four Seasons.

The journey will cross several continents

Guests onboard the jet will be taken care of by a dedicated journey team, which includes a concierge, physician and executive chef.

The route will start in San Francisco and take passengers across the Pacific to Seoul. While in the South Korean capital, guests will immerse themselves in spirituality at Jingwansa Temple.

Next up is Hangzhou in China, where guests will experience a tea ceremony at the Meijuawu Tea Plantation and spend time at the centuries-old Jinshan Temple.

A day trip to Shanghai will see passengers explore the city’s past and present with history expert Patrick Cranley.

Heading west, guests will arrive in Sri Lanka, where they’ll get to know the country’s heritage by following the journey of Ceylon cinnamon from harvest to quill and oil.

Four Seasons is set to open its Zanzibar-based resort in late 2027, and passengers on the jet will be amongst the first to experience it as part of a stop at this tropical archipelago of Tanzania.

Staying in Africa, guests will continue to Sharm El Sheikh, where they’ll board a private yacht charter to explore the Egyptian coastline.

After getting to know the Red Sea, passengers will be flown to the south of France for a stay in one of the glamorous French Riviera's most storied hotels, Grand-Hôtel du Cap-Ferrat, A Four Seasons Hotel.

From here, they’ll hop on another privately chartered yacht for an excursion to Cannes, world-famous for its film festival.

The trip ends with a hop across the English Channel with a stay at the Four Seasons Hotel Hampshire, in the south of the country. Guests will be able to relax in the English countryside and round off the epic journey with an exclusive visit to Henry VIII’s old haunt, Hampton Court Palace.

Other private jet experiences to consider

There are still a limited number of places available on some of Four Seasons’ 2027 private jet trips, for those who don’t want to wait until the following year.

Options include “international intrigue” (3–23 March), which combines cultural cities, remote islands and the African savannah, and “new world icons” (26 March–14 April), taking in landmarks and landscapes across Asia, Europe and the Americas.

Families can also book “world of adventures” (10 August–2 September), which travels across four continents, from the Seychelles to the Galápagos and beyond.

Meanwhile, “ancient explorer” (3–25 September) links historic sites and cultural highlights, including the Great Barrier Reef, Easter Island and the Pyramids of Giza.

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg and UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres blasted fossil fuel companies for "killing our planet".

Climate activist Greta Thunberg has blasted the annual COP climate summit as being hypocritical and "full of lobbyists".

Attending the talks for the first time since 2021, she urged leaders to put people and the planet ahead of profits and power.

The two-week COP31 talks kicked off in Turkey earlier this week with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal.

“It’s a hypocrisy every year that the host countries are given an opportunity to whitewash themselves and we know that these negotiations are filled with lobbyists, paid by the very destructive industries which are benefiting from our extremely violent status quo,” Thunberg said as she arrived. “Our political and economic systems that have become incompatible with human nature.”

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also spoke about these "very destructive industries" while addressing the conference: "Fossil fuel interests keep making a killing, while killing our planet," Guterres said, urging governments to tax the windfall profits of oil companies.

"Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won't happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do," he said.

'Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs'

"The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," Guterres told dozens of world leaders assembled at a sprawling expo centre in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.

But few major breakthroughs are anticipated at the COP31 negotiations, which run until 20 November, as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war with Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine.

Since agreeing in 2023 for the first time to transition away from fossil fuels - the main driver of climate change - nations have struggled to advance that goal at the annual COP conferences.

"Fossil fuel interests keep making a killing, while killing our planet," Guterres said, urging governments to tax the windfall profits of oil companies.

"Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won't happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do," he said.

"Their strategy is simple: Distort the science. Delay the policy. Delay the action. Delay the accountability. It's time to kick the habit – and end the fossil fuel addiction," he said to applause.

Guterres, who has made the fight against climate change a central issue since taking office in 2017, is attending his last COP before his term ends in December.

Greta Thunberg: 'Everything and everyone we love is at stake'

Electrification and waste reduction are set to be key focus points of this year's negotiations, which run until 20 November. Many EU countries are expected to advocate for the role of renewables and the transition away from fossil fuels, however the leaders of France, Germany, Italy and Spain have all been criticised for not attending the Leaders' Summit which runs today and tomorrow.

COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia are promoting renewable energy and rooftop solar installations, but both still rely heavily on fossil fuels, especially coal, to generate electricity. Previous hosts, including Brazil, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan, are major oil producers.

Climate change is “threatening everything,” Thunberg said, warning that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.”

“We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she said.

Thunberg blasts annual climate talks

This is the first climate summit Thunberg has attended since the 2021 talks in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed world leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah.”

She rose to prominence in 2018 when, aged 15, she began a solitary 'School Strike for Climate' outside the Swedish Parliament. In 2022, she published 'The Climate Book', outlining actions to address the climate crisis.

She has won multiple awards and advocated for other causes, including the Free Palestine movement. Last year, she was arrested in London while supporting hunger-striking pro-Palestinian activists. More recently, she supported French students protesting for more school resources.

In 2024, she joined a protest in Georgia against Azerbaijan’s hosting of COP29.

A key goal for Turkey is global electrification: shifting sectors such as transportation, buildings and heavy industry away from fossil fuels and toward electricity. Turkey wants electricity, preferably generated from renewable sources such as solar and wind, to account for 35 per cent of global energy consumption by 2035, up from 23 per cent today.

“We have to take the victories we have, of course, because we are so desperate in this situation that we have to take all the positive signs we can get to save as much as we can still save,” said Thunberg, who is expected to spend several days at COP31.

Youth activists rally around Thunberg

Thunberg's arrival at the conference created excitement among many youth climate activists.

“In this time of heightened geopolitical tensions, I hope that Greta’s presence here reminds us of why we started this work in the first place: to push for meaningful change, hold decision-makers accountable, and work towards a better future for all of humanity,” said Amber Turner, a 26-year-old fellow with the Alliance of Small Island States.

“Worsening climate change impacts make it challenging for young people to be sure of a safe and thriving future,” Turner added.

Protests at COP31 demanded more climate finance and criticised growing interest in nuclear energy.

“The presence of such a headline climate activist at one of the world’s biggest conferences on climate is symbolic, and I hope that it will put pressure on the COP itself to deliver real action and implementation,” said Kamori Osthananda, a youth negotiator with Thailand’s COP delegation.

Qiyun Woo, a youth environmentalist from Singapore, said Thunberg's “powerful” presence "adds to calls from a generation that inherits the consequences of these negotiations.”

“Besides her, there are many youth activists from around the world who are also on the ground who are actively fighting for their communities, home and collective future,” she said.

A second claim brought under a Florida consumer protection law was thrown out, halving the original $10bn lawsuit to $5bn, but the US president has still hailed the ruling as “A Huge Victory”.

A US judge has rejected the BBC's motion to dismiss Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against the broadcaster allowing the case to proceed to trial.

The US president's claim is based on the way the BBC edited a speech he gave on 6 January 2021 in its Panorama documentary.

On Tuesday, US District Judge Jeffrey T. Kuntz denied the British broadcaster’s attempt to have the defamation claim dismissed. He did, however, throw out a second claim, which Trump had brought under Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

Each claim was for at least $5bn (€4.48bn), meaning Kuntz's ruling halves the lawsuit from $10 billion (€8.97bn) to at least $5 billion.

The case centres on a BBC documentary that spliced together two separate parts of the speech. The edit made it appear that Trump had explicitly urged his supporters to attack the US Capitol in Washington. Trump accuses the broadcaster of deceptively editing the programme to make it look as though he was inciting violence.

In his 40-page ruling, Kuntz wrote: “Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day.”

But he said the gap between the two spliced sections pointed to deliberate distortion.

“Given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement,” Kuntz wrote.

“This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech.”

A BBC spokesperson said: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process."

Trump ordered to testify by December

Congo's Ebola outbreak has become the deadliest in the country's history, with more than 11,000 cases and over 5,000 deaths recorded so far as conflict, strikes and mistrust hamper response.

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has reached 11,042 cases and 5,387 deaths — almost half of those infected — making it the country’s deadliest, according to the latest government data from Wednesday.

This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in Congo and the fastest-growing in the country’s history. It surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of the response being activated. By comparison, the 2018 outbreak took about 235 days to pass 1,000 cases.

The ongoing outbreak, which was officially declared in May, continues to spread and remains difficult to tackle due to ongoing armed conflict, a crisis in the health system, poor roads and violence from residents fuelled by mistrust and misinformation.

Unpaid salaries and strikes by workers are complicating the response further, paralysing key facilities in several regions and forcing work to stop at numerous screening checkpoints along transport axes, at river ports, on municipal borders and at airports, the Health Ministry said.

A resurgence of violence by armed groups in the two main hotspots, Ituri and North Kivu provinces, has alarmed health authorities, who are calling for an end to the fighting so that health workers can reach the sick without obstacle.

The Ministry also warned that mistrust is a major obstacle to containing the outbreak, showing itself in harmful rumours, high rates of refusal of health screenings, resistance to safe burials and falling attendance at health facilities.

In some cases, the mistrust among local communities fuels violence against medical personnel and facilities, which is also hampering operations, shutting down several response points across the country, including in Ituri, the epicentre of the outbreak.

No approved vaccine, but trials are under way

The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no approved vaccine or treatment, although several trials are under way.

The World Health Organization (WHO) backed two vaccine candidates last week: one developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, the other by Moderna. The trial will be led by the Democratic Republic of Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research, with support from international partners, including the WHO.

‘Vaccines are powerful tools, but they’re not substitutes for the proven measures that can save lives now,’ WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said at the press conference announcing the trials on 4 November, citing early care, contact tracing, isolation, safe and dignified burials and trusted engagement with communities.

Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first identified in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.

Best known for his roles in movies like 'Fat City', 'The Ninth Configuration' and TV shows like The New Mike Hammer and Prison Break, Keach was a formidable presence on both stage and screen.

American stage and screen actor Stacy Keach, best known for his roles in movies like Fat City, The Ninth Configuration and TV shows The New Mike Hammer and Prison Break, has died aged 85.

His wife, Małgosia Tomassi, confirmed his death, saying in a statement (via Variety) that her husband died “after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure” at the family’s home in Magdalenka, Poland.

“Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family,” the statement said. “His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever."

Born in Savannah, Georgia, Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.

In the summer of 1963, he worked with the Oregon Shakespeare Festival and played Henry V, Mercutio and Lord Berowne.

He attended the Yale School of Drama and, in the summer of 1964, played several roles at New York’s Public Theater in Hamlet with Julie Harris. He went to study at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art as a Fulbright scholar and returned to New York to do various stage roles.

Keach's career spanned stage and screen, and while he will be fondly remembered for playing the scruffy private eye Mike Hammer, his on screen work showed he could take on any role.

From The Ninth Configuration (also known as Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane), his work for director John Huston in Fat City and The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean, his Golden Globe-winning portrayal of Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, to American History X, The Bourne Legacy and Alexander Payne’s Oscar-nominated drama Nebraska, Keach was a varied and commanding presence. His final role was as George Clooney’s bitter father in Jay Kelly.

“My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career,” he told New York magazine in 2012. “My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I’ve gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything.”

His career was nearly derailed in 1984 while he was still doing Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer (later titled The New Mike Hammer). Keach was arrested at London’s Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle cocaine in his luggage.

“As my sentence was read – nine months in prison – I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats,” he wrote in his 2013 book, "All in All: An Actor’s Life On and Off the Stage". “It was the lowest moment of my life.”

Keach was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, and was released after six months.

Many years later, in the TV series Prison Break that aired from 2005 to 2017, Keach played a prison warden. He said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help prisoners rehabilitate themselves.

Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the Hammer series, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.

RIP Stacy Keach 1941 - 2026
